peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Reviewers
We sincerely thank the Editors and Reviewers once again for their valuable time, meticulous re-evaluation, and insightful supplementary feedback. We have carefully considered every additional comment and have revised the manuscript accordingly. We believe these revisions have further strengthened the rigor, completeness, and clarity of our work. Below, we provide a detailed point-by-point response to each comment. All changes and supplementary content in the revised manuscript are highlighted for easy reference.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have substantially and thoughtfully addressed nearly all 15 of the raised concerns. Their rebuttal includes new experimental data (e.g., longitudinal lactate measurements, collagen immunofluorescence, PK/PD profiles), mechanistic clarifications (Zdhhc13-mediated palmitoylation, Cbx3 transcriptional repression), and translational considerations (clinical serum lactate data, safety/tissue distribution of LNPs).
While the responses are comprehensive, a few areas could still be strengthened, including:
1. More detailed quantitative analyses (effect sizes, fibrosis morphometry, longitudinal statistics).
Response: We sincerely appreciate your positive recognition of our comprehensive revisions and constructive feedback on further strengthening the manuscript’s quantitative rigor. We fully agree that detailed quantitative analyses are essential to reinforcing the reliability and biological relevance of our findings.
As requested, we have supplemented detailed longitudinal statistical analyses for cavernosal lactate and intracavernous pressure. The results confirm a statistically significant increase over time in the DMED group. These new analyses are presented in Supplementary Figures 1d-1f, and described in the main text.
In direct response to your suggestion, we have now calculated and reported effect sizes for key quantitative comparisons. For comparisons between two groups using the unpaired t-test, we calculated Cohen's d value, as it is the most appropriate and widely accepted measure of standardized effect size for this statistical test. It provides a clear interpretation of the magnitude of the difference between groups, independent of sample size. For one-way ANOVA analyses involving multiple groups, we first calculated the overall effect size using eta-squared (η²) and reported the Cohen's d value for the relevant pairwise post-hoc comparisons. The values are now reported in the respective figure legends. Additionally, we have supplemented sample sizes (n values) and detailed statistical methods in the panel of each figure legend, ensuring full transparency for reproducibility.
We sincerely thank you for your valuable suggestion regarding the need for detailed fibrosis morphometric analysis. In response, we conducted a systematic and in-depth re-analysis of our existing histology and immunofluorescence images. Upon careful examination, we found that our results are consistent with the majority of existing reports in this research field [PMID: 36064453;32693824；38874549；39536767； 37157936]. In the DMED model, the core characteristic of fibrotic deposition is a significant quantitative increase in collagen content, whereas under the resolution of our current methodologies (conventional histological staining), no consistent or significant differences in the higher-order architecture (i.e., morphology) were detected. We fully understand and agree with your insightful perspective that more subtle morphological differences may require more advanced techniques for detection. The absence of observed significant morphological changes in this study may indeed reflect the detection limits of the conventional methods we employed.
We sincerely thank you for your insightful guidance, which has helped us refine the quantitative presentation of our findings, standardize statistical reporting, and clarify the nature of fibrosis-related changes in our model—further enhancing the rigor and comprehensiveness of our work.
2. Additional causal validation (e.g., autophagy inhibition rescue, metabolic flux tracing).
Response: We sincerely appreciate the valuable suggestion regarding the necessity of supplementing causal validation experiments. We fully concur that in-depth mechanistic verification is pivotal for establishing the pathophysiological association between lactate and DMED.
In the previous revision round, transcriptome sequencing revealed that lactate treatment activates the autophagic pathway in CCSMCs. In response to your recommendation, we have performed more rigorous causal validation in the current revision.
In vitro experiments were conducted by pretreating CCSMCs with the autophagy inhibitor 3-methyladenine (3-MA). The results demonstrated that 3-MA significantly abrogates lactate-induced excessive autophagy activation, impairment of cell viability, and phenotypic switching toward the synthetic smooth muscle phenotype.
In animal models, we further analyzed autophagic activity in the corpus cavernosum of lactate-challenged mice and DMED mice. Intriguingly, progressive elevation of the LC3-II/LC3-I ratio was observed in both models during disease progression, whereas P62 protein expression exhibited a dynamic change characterized by an initial decrease followed by a subsequent increase. This finding suggests that autophagic flux may become dysregulated in the late stage of the disease.
Building upon these observations, we performed interventions with 3-MA and SMER28, respectively. Our data showed that 3-MA effectively suppressed excessive autophagy and remarkably improved erectile function as well as tissue architecture in DMED mice. In contrast, although SMER28 promoted P62 degradation, it failed to exert significant therapeutic efficacy.
Finally, we validated that Fbp1 C282S-LNP treatment can also efficiently reverse autophagic abnormalities in the corpus cavernosum of DMED mice.
Collectively, these results indicate that lactate-induced excessive autophagy is a key mechanism contributing to corpus cavernosum smooth muscle cell damage.
Furthermore, CCSMCs were cultured with 2 mM ¹³C-labeled lactate under starvation conditions, and the extracellular medium was analyzed by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy referring to relevant literature [PMID：12944325, PMID： 10751328, PMID：10600777]. We successfully detected the production of ¹³C-labeled glucose, which directly confirms that CCSMCs possess gluconeogenic capacity to convert lactate into glucose. This finding provides direct experimental evidence supporting the central role of lactate metabolism in CCSMCs.
3. Longer-term follow-up and repeat-dose safety data to enhance translational relevance.
Response:We are grateful for this insightful comment regarding the long-term safety profile and therapeutic sustainability of the Fbp1 C282S-LNP strategy, which represent key considerations for its clinical translation. In our previous revision, a preliminary assessment of treatment durability was conducted, incorporating a one-month treatment-free observation period following the initial 4-week therapy. It is noteworthy that the principal therapeutic benefits—including improved lactate metabolism, tissue repair, and erectile function—were consistently maintained throughout this follow-up interval (Supplementary Figure 16). These observations suggest that the intervention may promote sustained and restorative outcomes beyond transient symptomatic amelioration.
We fully concur that a more systematic evaluation of long-term safety and repeated dosing regimens is essential to further de-risk this therapeutic strategy. A study designed to comprehensively address these aspects would require an extended timeline with multiple treatment cycles and detailed systemic toxicity monitoring, which lies beyond the scope of the present discovery-phase investigation.
In response to your suggestion, we have added a dedicated paragraph in the Discussion section to acknowledge this direction and outline future work: "Although sustained treatment effects were observed following short-term intervention in this study, further investigation is warranted to elucidate the long-term safety profile and optimal dosing frequency of Fbp1 C282S-LNP. Subsequent studies employing extended multi-dose regimens in larger animal models will be valuable to comprehensively assess chronic toxicity and maximize the translational potential of this strategy."
We thank you again for this suggestion, which has enhanced the clinical relevance and scholarly rigor of our work.
4. Schematic figures in the introduction or discussion to better communicate the proposed mechanism.
Overall, the revisions substantially improve the manuscript, and the study now provides a clearer mechanistic insight and stronger therapeutic rationale for targeting Fbp1/lactate metabolism in DMED. I believe the paper is much closer to being suitable for publication after minor additional clarifications.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the suggestion to add a schematic diagram in the main text for a clearer presentation of the mechanism pathway. In response to your recommendation, we have inserted a fully annotated mechanism schematic (Figure 8) along with relevant textual explanations in the Discussion section of the paper:
Transcriptional repression and functional dysfunction of Fbp1 are key causes of penile cavernosal lactate accumulation in DMED. Mechanistically, H3K9me3 mediated by the Suv39h1/Cbx3 complex and H3K27me3 mediated by Ezh2 cooperatively suppress Fbp1 transcription; meanwhile, Zdhhc13-mediated palmitoylation of the FBP1 protein at the C282 site directly impairs its gluconeogenic function, exacerbating lactate accumulation. To target the aforementioned aberrant mechanisms, we developed Fbp1 C282S-LNP, which restores Fbp1 expression and blocks pathological palmitoylation via intracavernosal injection, thereby effectively reducing local lactate levels.
We believe that the inclusion of this schematic diagram significantly enhances the visual presentation of the mechanism pathway in the paper, enabling readers to more intuitively comprehend the logical connection between the molecular mechanisms and the therapeutic strategy. We sincerely thank you again for this valuable suggestion, which has played a crucial role in improving the quality of the paper.
Reviewer #6 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Xiao et al identifies fructose 1,6 bisphosphatase 1 (FBP1) activity in corpus cavernosum smooth muscle cells (CCSMCs) as a potentially important component to erectile function in mice and the overall health of CCSMCs. This is by virtue of FBP1's role in the gluconeogenic pathway, which the authors claim is necessary to prevent lactate accumulation that may otherwise impair CCSMC function. The implications are significant because this study provides a potentially novel target for ED treatment that could in theory be used alone or in conjunction with traditional therapies such as phosphodiesterase inhibitors.
The authors report that FBP1 expression and function in CCSMCs is reduced in a model of diabetes mellitus-induced erectile dysfuncton(DMED). This happens as a result of epigenetic and post-translational events, leading ultimately to elevated lactate concentrations in the corpus cavernosum. The authors go to great lengths to identify the mechanistic basis for changes in FBP1 expression (via histone methylation pathways) and functon(via palmitoylation), using in vitro methods as well as their mouse model of DMED. The molecular biology experiments are fairly thorough by design (although underpowered), and complimentary approaches are used. In particular, the use of lipid nanoparticles to deliver palmitoylation-resistant FBP1 is a compelling approach to correct aberrant metabolic processes.
While concerns raised by Reviewer 2 on palmitoylation were adequately addressed by authors, there are several major issues, described below, which diminish the overall impact of the manuscript. In general, while many of the experiments shed light on the regulatory mechanisms controlling the functional expression of FBP1 in various systems, extrapolation of these findings to the author's central hypothesis is limited by several concerns.
Major concerns:
1 - The central hypothesis of the manuscript rests on the idea that dysregulation of FBP1 in CCSMCs leads to lactate accumulation via suppression of gluconeogenesis. However, the authors do not provide evidence, nor do they cite previous work showing that CCSMCs actually carry out gluconeogenesis to a significant degree. Aside from transcript-level data and a western blot showing that a few other gluconeogenic enzymes were not altered the corpus cavernosum of DMED mice (Sup Fig 2), there is no supporting evidence that lactate accumulation in the corpus cavernosum happens as a result impaired flux through the gluconeogenic pathway within CCSMCs. Relying on the quantification of enzyme abundance, rather than measuring glucose or metabolite production directly, is not a rigorous way to test the extent to which glycolytic or gluconeogenic pathways proceed in CCSMCs under the experimental conditions. Without a clear demonstration that CCSMCs carry out gluconeogenesis and that inhibition of this pathway specifically leads to lactate accumulation, it is impossible to interpret the study's findings in the context of the authors' proposed model. The authors must definitively show that CCSMC-localized FB1 participates in "lactate clearance via gluconeogenesis," so to speak, otherwise the premise of the study is not sound.
The authors do mention that conversion of lactate into glucose via the Cori Cycle is a key part of lactate metabolism. However, in this pathway, lactate generated by muscle under anaerobic conditions is converted to glucose in the liver. If a similar pathway exists within smooth muscle cells, the authors should include a reference which describes it. Likewise, many of the references to FBP1 function in lactate metabolism and/or diabetic models involve studies using liver cells or liver tissue. It is not appropriate to draw parallels between the findings of this study and others that deal with these pathways specifically in the liver.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful comments. You correctly noted that establishing the functional gluconeogenic capacity of corpus cavernosum smooth muscle cells (CCSMCs) is a core premise of this study. To address this, we have reviewed foundational work in the field and integrated our experimental data to provide the following systematic evidence:
Smooth muscle cells have been shown to possess complete gluconeogenic capacity and independent gluconeogenic metabolic compartments [PMID: 8789645]. Fbp1, a key functional enzyme in this pathway, catalyzes the critical conversion of exogenous fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to glucose [PMID: 10600777] and exhibits unique subcellular localization in smooth muscle cells [PMID: 16200456]. Pathological studies further underscore Fbp1’s functional importance—for instance, downregulation of gluconeogenic enzymes (including Fbp1) during vascular calcification correlates closely with metabolic imbalance [PMID: 21757657].
Collectively, these findings confirm Fbp1 as a functional, indispensable key enzyme for gluconeogenesis in smooth muscle cells. Unlike hepatic gluconeogenesis (which maintains systemic glucose homeostasis), CCSMC gluconeogenesis may support local energy demands (e.g., during erection) or clear lactate (preventing local acidosis-induced impairment of smooth muscle contraction).
Second, building on this theoretical framework, we provide direct experimental evidence via metabolic flux analysis. Primary mouse CCSMCs were cultured with 2 mM ¹³C-labeled lactate under starvation conditions; nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) detected ¹³C-labeled glucose production, directly confirming CCSMCs’ gluconeogenic capacity.
More importantly, we established a complete causal evidence chain in animal models: (1) DMED models showed reduced Fbp1 expression and lactate accumulation in cavernous tissue; (2) Fbp1+/- mice exhibited significantly elevated cavernous lactate levels; (3) Fbp1 C282S-LNP was extensively taken up by CCSMCs, restoring functional Fbp1 expression in cavernous tissue, reducing lactate levels, and improving erectile function.
Additionally, analyses of oxygen consumption rate (OCR), extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), and glucose/lactate production flux in the MOVAS cell line further support Fbp1’s critical role in regulating smooth muscle cell metabolic homeostasis. However, we acknowledge that limitations in primary cell acquisition prevented replication of some energy metabolism experiments in primary cells—an inherent constraint of primary cell research.
In summary, through systematic literature review, direct metabolic flux validation, and in vitro/in vivo functional experiments, we provide multi-level evidence for our core hypothesis: "Impaired FBP1 function in CCSMCs causes lactate accumulation by inhibiting gluconeogenesis." Thank you for your valuable input, which has strengthened the rigor of our argument.
2 - Throughout the study, elevations in lactate concentration, either systemically or locally, are reported in association with functional/structural/biochemical changes in the corpus cavernosum. However, these observations are correlative and there is a lack of evidence suggesting the downstream effects are a direct result of lactate accumulation consequent to suppressed gluconeogenesis/FBP1 activity within CCSMCs. In addition, there should be more discussion of how excessive lactate might cause the phenotypic effects that are described. What is the underlying pathological mechanism by which lactate accumulation causes dysfunction?
Response: We sincerely appreciate this important comment of yours. You correctly pointed out the need to clarify the causal relationship between lactate accumulation and the observed functional dysfunction, as well as to further elaborate on its underlying pathological mechanism. We have addressed this issue through supplementary experiments and in-depth discussions.
To confirm that the observed phenotypic changes are a direct consequence of lactate accumulation, we conducted gain-of-function and rescue experiments both in vitro and in vivo:In in vitro experiments, we treated CCSMCs with exogenous sodium lactate (5 mM and 10 mM). The results showed that key pathological changes—including decreased cell viability and phenotypic switching—exhibited a dose-dependent pattern, demonstrating lactate’s direct damaging effect. In animal experiments, intraperitoneal injection of sodium lactate into healthy mice successfully increased lactate levels in the corpus cavernosum, accompanied by significant impairment of erectile function and histological changes that recapitulated the core pathological features of DMED. Most compellingly, targeted restoration of Fbp1 function in the corpus cavernosum using Fbp1 C282S-LNPs effectively reduced lactate accumulation and reversed both erectile dysfunction and tissue damage in DMED mice. This rescue experiment confirms that correcting lactate metabolic dysregulation is sufficient to improve the disease phenotype.
We fully understand and highly agree with your insightful suggestion regarding the need to further strengthen the evidence chain for lactate’s downstream mechanism of action—this profound perspective helps establish a causal link confirming that lactate accumulation is a direct cause of cavernous dysfunction.
In the previous revision, transcriptome sequencing revealed that lactate treatment activates the autophagic pathway in CCSMCs.
Following your recommendation, we performed more rigorous mechanistic validation in the current revision:
In vitro experiments demonstrated that the autophagy inhibitor 3-methyladenine (3-MA) significantly suppressed lactate-induced excessive autophagy, impaired cell viability, and phenotypic switching.
Animal experiments further showed that in both lactate-challenged mice and DMED mice, the ratio of the autophagy marker LC3-II/LC3-I was elevated, while P62 protein expression exhibited dynamic changes—suggesting dysregulated autophagic flux.
Intervention experiments revealed that the autophagy inhibitor 3-MA effectively improved erectile function and tissue structure in DMED mice, whereas the autophagy enhancer SMER28, despite promoting P62 degradation, exerted no significant therapeutic effect.
Finally, we validated that Fbp1 C282S-LNP treatment can also efficiently reverse autophagic abnormalities in the corpus cavernosum of DMED mice.
These results indicate that lactate-induced excessive autophagy is a key mechanism underlying corpus cavernosum smooth muscle cell damage.
We believe that these newly supplemented experimental data, together with our existing evidence, form a complete causal evidence chain, clearly defining the pathological mechanism: "lactate accumulation → excessive autophagy → cell damage → functional dysfunction." We again thank you for your valuable comments, which have played a pivotal role in enhancing the mechanistic depth of our study.
3 - Do the authors suggest that lactate is produced in CCSMCs under aerobic conditions? Does oxygen availability in corpus cavernosum have an impact on lactate generation? Is it possible that aerobic metabolism is somehow impaired in CCSMCs in the DMED model, and that this leads to lactate accumulation independently of FBP1? If there are other metabolic disturbances in CCSMCs in the DMED model, the mechanism(s) leading to lactate accumulation may or may not be connected to the functional impairment of the corpus cavernosum. As mentioned above, it would be helpful to discuss a clear mechanistic link between excessive lactate and impaired CCSMC function.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the series of profound questions you raised, which have been crucial for refining the demonstration of metabolic mechanisms in this study.
First, regarding lactate production under aerobic conditions, previous studies have indeed shown that even under aerobic conditions, normal metabolic activity generates small amounts of lactate due to the metabolic compartmentalization of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis in cells—though lactate production increases significantly under hypoxic conditions. We also fully acknowledge that oxygen supply to the corpus cavernosum is a important factor influencing lactate levels, and several studies have confirmed that the pathological process of DMED is closely associated with local hypoxia.
Your question regarding "whether other metabolic disorders contribute to lactate accumulation in the DMED model" is highly insightful. We honestly acknowledge that this study focuses on elucidating the mechanism of reduced lactate clearance mediated by FBP1 dysfunction. Our data—such as the downregulated transcriptional levels of key glycolytic enzymes—indicate that in the DMED model used in this study, lactate accumulation is more likely driven by impaired clearance. Additionally, we attempted to inhibit glycolysis using an LDHA inhibitor, but this did not significantly reduce cavernous lactate levels. Of course, we cannot completely rule out the possibility of other pathways (e.g., impaired aerobic metabolism), and these complex metabolic interactions undoubtedly represent important directions for future research.
Nevertheless, our series of functional experiments strongly confirm that the FBP1-mediated lactate metabolic pathway plays an indispensable core role in DMED: manipulating FBP1 function directly affects lactate levels, and restoring FBP1 function via Fbp1 C282S-LNPs specifically improves local lactate metabolism and rescues erectile function. This demonstrates that this pathway is a sufficient and important cause of functional dysfunction.
Finally, we fully agree with your insight that a clear mechanistic link between excessive lactate and impaired CCSMC function must be established. This was one of the core focuses of our current revision. As addressed in the previous response, following your suggestion, we confirmed through experiments that lactate-induced excessive autophagy is the key link in the causal chain connecting these two processes, and we have included an in-depth discussion of this mechanism.
We again thank you for your insightful questions, which have greatly enhanced the logical rigor and mechanistic depth of our study.
4 - In the model of the heterozygous Fbp1-/+ mice, genetic disruption is global, making it difficult to parse out local effects in the corpus cavernosum from effects elsewhere in the body (i.e., the liver). Is it possible that metabolic disruption from global Fbp1-/+ produces the functional changes in CCSMCs as part of a broader systemic phenotype? Is it possible that CCSMC dysfunction happens coincidentally with an elevation in circulating lactate, but not necessarily because of it? This does not rule out the possibility that elevated circulating lactate in Fbp1-/+ mice has a detrimental effect on CCSMCs, but it is difficult to justify the conclusion that CCSMC-localized FBP1 dysregulation is driving the observed effects.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate this profound, critical question. Your insight into the limitations of the Fbp1+/- heterozygous mouse model—and concern about potential confounding between systemic metabolic disorders and local effects—are entirely reasonable and well-founded. This has prompted us to interpret our conclusions more cautiously and strengthen support for the local mechanism with supplementary experiments.
You correctly noted that in the systemic Fbp1+/- model, distinguishing between cavernous local effects and systemic impacts (e.g., hyperlactatemia from impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis) is challenging. Systemically elevated lactate could independently exert direct toxic effects on corpus cavernosum smooth muscle cells (CCSMCs), causing dysfunction. We fully agree that phenotypic data from Fbp1+/- mice alone would be insufficient to conclude "local FBP1 dysfunction in CCSMCs drives the phenotype."
It is noteworthy that we observed elevated plasma lactate levels in clinical patients with DMED, and lactate concentration was significantly correlated with both the occurrence and severity of the condition. In a DMED mouse model, we similarly found increased lactate levels in both plasma and penile tissues. Through in vivo and in vitro experiments, we further validated the dose-dependent detrimental effect of lactate on CCSMCs and erectile function. More importantly, after administration of Fbp1-C282S-LNP, tissue distribution analysis revealed that the nanoparticles preferentially accumulated in the corpus cavernosum, where they were efficiently taken up by CCSMCs. This led to a significant reduction in intracavernosal lactate levels and a marked improvement in the erectile function phenotype of DMED mice.
In the current round of experiments, we further added immunofluorescence staining and quantitative tissue analysis of the liver, skeletal muscle, and penile corpus cavernosum. Crucially, pharmacokinetic data first showed Fbp1 C282S-LNPs (administered via local cavernous injection) were primarily retained in the injected penis. While minor accumulation was detected in the liver and skeletal muscle over time, the combined results of immunofluorescence staining and quantitative tissue analysis confirmed that only the penile corpus cavernosum exhibited a statistically significant increase in Fbp1 protein expression—no significant changes were observed in the liver or skeletal muscle.
These results strongly suggest that elevated lactate levels localized in the corpus cavernosum impair CCSMC function and erectile function, and that the corresponding therapeutic effect is primarily driven by the specific upregulation of FBP1 within the cavernous tissue, rather than indirect systemic metabolic modulation. We fully agree with your emphasis on methodological rigor, which has helped us sharpen the focus and strengthen the core argument of our study. Relevant clarifications have been incorporated into the revised manuscript, and we thank you again for your insightful feedback.
5 - Apomorphine, the drug used to induce erection in mice, is a centrally acting dopamine receptor agonist targeting dopamine signaling pathways in the brain. It is thought to be most effective for psychogenic erectile dysfuncton(in humans) and works via a mechanism separate from PDE inhibitors, which act locally. How do the authors rule out that experimental interventions (DMED model, lactate injection, metabolic changes from Fbp1-/+, etc.) do not interfere with neural control of erectile function?
Response: We sincerely appreciate the important question you raised. You correctly pointed out that apomorphine, as a central dopamine receptor agonist, induces erections primarily by activating dopamine signaling pathways in the central nervous system—this mechanism differs from the local action of PDE5 inhibitors. We fully agree that excluding potential interference of experimental interventions on the neural control pathway of erections is crucial for ensuring the reliability of our study’s conclusions.
We can clearly rule out such interference through the following experimental design and results:
First, in the different animal models involved in this study, the use of apomorphine was strictly limited to baseline screening of erectile function in DMED model mice (i.e., administered only once after model establishment and before grouping for intervention). This step was used to verify whether the animals had successfully developed an ED model and possessed inducible erectile potential, which is a commonly used method in DMED model establishment [PMID: 41090037; 40676888; 39654344]. In contrast, in the Fbp1+/- mouse model and the lactate injection model, apomorphine was not used at any stage from the start to the end of the experiment. Instead, changes in erectile function were evaluated using intracavernous pressure (ICP) measurements and histological examinations. Therefore, the changes in erectile function observed in these latter two model groups can completely exclude interference from the central effects of apomorphine, and their results directly reflect the independent impact of metabolic alterations (Fbp1 deficiency or exogenous lactate) on erectile function.
Second, during the screening phase of the DMED model, we ensured strict consistency in experimental procedures. After receiving apomorphine (100 μg/kg, subcutaneous injection). The positive erectile rate in the normal control group was nearly 100%, which strongly confirms that the central neural pathway dependent on apomorphine was functionally intact under our experimental conditions. If DMED or its associated metabolic interventions (e.g., lactate accumulation) had impaired this neural pathway, delayed or absent erectile responses should have been observed first in the control group or during the early screening phase—but this was not the case. This indicates that DMED-related erectile dysfunction does not originate from primary damage to the neural control pathway.
Finally, regarding concerns about drug residue effects, apomorphine has an extremely short elimination half-life in mice. After a single screening injection, the drug was completely cleared long before the start of the 4-week intervention treatment with Fbp1 C282S-LNP and other agents. Therefore, all subsequent therapeutic effects were significantly associated with the restoration of local FBP1 activity and the reduction of lactate levels in the corpus cavernosum. This series of results clearly indicates that the mechanism of action stems from the correction of the local metabolic environment, rather than sustained effects on the neural pathway revealed by the early apomorphine test.
We again thank you for your profound insight, which has made our argument more rigorous.
Minor concerns
1 - The authors describe H-PROTAC as a CBX3-sepcific degrader. However, Supp Fig 5 does not demonstrate specificity. The authors did not test whether degradation of other proteins, aside from CBX3, were altered by H-PROTAC treatment.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the important question you raised regarding the specificity verification of H-PROTAC. You correctly pointed out that our description of H-PROTAC as a "CBX3-specific degrader" in the original manuscript was insufficiently rigorous, and Supplementary Figure 9 indeed failed to fully demonstrate its selectivity for other proteins.
As stated in our Methods section, we screened protein databases and identified that the QTAR M3L peptide of H3K9me3 can specifically bind to CBX3—based on this finding, we developed a degrader primarily targeting CBX3. However, we fully agree that since CBX1, CBX3, and CBX5 all belong to the HP1 family and are all H3K9me3 readers, this degrader may indeed exhibit a certain degree of cross-reactivity.
In accordance with your suggestion, we have supplemented experiments to verify the degradation effect of H-PROTAC on different CBX protein family members. The results showed that at a concentration of 1 μM, H-PROTAC significantly degraded CBX3, while its degradation effect on CBX1 and CBX5 was notably weaker. This concentration gradient experiment not only provided a basis for us to select the optimal working concentration but also confirmed that H-PROTAC exhibits relative selectivity for CBX3 at specific concentrations.
We have revised the relevant description in the original manuscript, and supplemented the corresponding experimental data. These revisions have made our descriptions more accurate and our experimental design more comprehensive. We once again thank you for your rigorous review comments, which are of great value for improving the scientific rigor and accuracy of our research.
2 - Experiments assessing the palmitoylation status of FBP1 should include both positive and negative controls (proteins known to be palmitoylated and known to not be palmitoylated) to demonstrate that the assay was successful. In addition, there should be quantitation for these experiments, and not just a representative immunoblot.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the critical comment emphasizing the necessity of including positive/negative controls and performing quantitative analysis in experiments investigating FBP1 palmitoylation. We fully concur that these recommendations are essential for ensuring the reliability of experimental results, and systematic refinements have been implemented in the previous round of revisions.
Specifically, in the acyl-biotin exchange (ABE) assay—a gold-standard method for detecting protein palmitoylation—we have established a comprehensive control system: acylglycerol kinase (AGK), a well-characterized stably palmitoylated protein, was employed as the positive control, while β-actin (for which no evidence of palmitoylation has been reported to date) served as the negative control. This control strategy robustly validates the efficacy of our experimental protocol.
Concurrently, rigorous quantitative analysis of palmitoylation levels was performed across all cell line-based experiments. The full set of quantitative results has been compiled in Supplementary Figure S11, thereby providing reliable data support for our experimental findings. It should be noted that in primary cell experiments, quantitative analysis is subject to certain limitations due to practical constraints, including the difficulty in isolating primary cells and the restricted number of viable cell passages.
Through these supplementary experiments and methodological refinements, we believe the current experimental data substantially enhance the reliability and persuasiveness of our FBP1 palmitoylation detection results. We would like to express our gratitude again to the reviewer for this valuable guidance, which plays a pivotal role in improving the methodological rigor of the present study.
3 - Typically, palmitoylation of proteins is thought to promote an interaction with lipid membranes. Are there other examples of palmitoylation causing structural/functional changes in cytosolic enzymes? If so, this should be discussed.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the profound question you raised. You correctly pointed out that palmitoylation modification is generally considered to promote the interaction between proteins and lipid membranes. The recent studies have indeed revealed that palmitoylation can also directly induce conformational changes in cytoplasmic enzymes, thereby regulating their activity—and this is highly consistent with the phenomenon we observed in FBP1 [PMID: 16945566; PMID: 16128592; PMID: 25576832].
In accordance with your suggestion, we have supplemented the relevant literature and discussions in the Discussion section of the paper. These precedents strongly support our finding that Zdhhc13-mediated palmitoylation at the C282 site can induce conformational changes in FBP1, thereby affecting the accessibility of its active center and ultimately inhibiting the gluconeogenic function of this enzyme. We sincerely thank you for this directional suggestion, as it has placed our research in a broader theoretical context and significantly enhanced the depth of our discussion.
4 - In general, the figure legends and in-text figure descriptions require much more detailed information. Figure legends in particular should have details of the experimental conditions, spelled out acronyms for the text in the figure panels, description of the assays used for generation of each panel within the figure, description of the statistical tests used, etc. Also many of the experiments have an n=3. A larger sample size would increase the rigor of the study.
Response:We sincerely appreciate the valuable suggestions regarding the improvement of figure information and the increase in sample size. We fully agree that detailed figure legends and an adequate sample size are crucial for ensuring the reproducibility and rigor of the study, and comprehensive revisions have been made in accordance with the reviewer’s comments.
To address the issue of insufficiently detailed figure information, we have systematically refined all figure legends: each legend now explicitly supplements key experimental methods corresponding to individual subfigures, experimental conditions, statistical methods, sample size, and the full names of all abbreviations used in the figures. This ensures that readers can accurately understand the details of each experimental design and analytical approach.
Regarding the sample size concern, we sincerely accept your comment. In all new experiments conducted during this round of revisions, the sample size has been increased to n=5. Meanwhile, it should be noted that due to constraints in experimental timeline and resources, we were unable to supplement the sample size for experiments already completed in the manuscript. We acknowledge that this may affect the statistical power of some study results, for which we sincerely apologize, and this limitation has been described in the " Limitations" section of the paper.
These improvements have significantly enhanced the transparency, reproducibility, and credibility of our study results. We would like to thank the reviewer again for the insightful suggestions, which have played an important role in improving the quality of our research work.
5 - Line 75-80: The previous observation that sildenafil reduced lactate accumulation in exercising rats does not necessarily imply a connection between lactate metabolism and erectile function. It only suggests that PDE5 inhibition reduces lactate accumulation caused be strenuous exercise.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the important insight. You are absolutely correct that the previously cited observation regarding sildenafil reducing lactate accumulation in exercised rats cannot directly establish a mechanistic link between lactate metabolism and erectile function—it merely demonstrates that PDE5 inhibition can alleviate lactate accumulation induced by strenuous exercise. In accordance with your suggestion, we have deleted the potentially misleading statements in the original manuscript. We sincerely thank you for this highly insightful correction, as this revision has significantly enhanced the logical rigor of our discussion.
REVIEWERS' COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Our concerns have been addressed in the revisions.so now we have no additional question.
Response: We are very grateful for your time and careful review of our manuscript. Your guidance has helped improve our manuscript. Thank you again for your support and comments.
Reviewer #6 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have satisfactorily addressed the concerns raised from the previous review. They have added citations describing the capacity of smooth muscle cells to participate in gluconeogenesis, as well as provided experimental evidence of glucose production in CCSM cells. They have established a more clear mechanistic link between lactate accumulation and CCSM cells dysfuncton(via autophagy). They have appropriately acknowledged the limitations of using a global Fbp1-/+ mouse model in terms of parsing out local versus systemic effects in the corpus cavernosum. They included more controls in their CBX3 degradation assays, and added information to all figure legends to improve clarity. I have no further suggestions for improving the manuscript.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your valuable time and meticulous review of our revised manuscript. Thank you again for your support and comments.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The high prevalence of diabetes mellitus-induced erectile dysfunction (DMED) in males and the limited efficacy of existing therapies necessitate deeper mechanistic insights. We identify pathological lactate accumulation in the corpus cavernosum as a major driver of DMED in male mice, promoting structural degeneration and smooth muscle cell loss. Mechanistically, transcriptional repression and functional impairment of fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (Fbp1), a rate-limiting gluconeogenic enzyme, underlie this lactate accumulation. Epigenetic profiling revealed suppression of Fbp1 transcription associated with histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation and histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation. Palmitoylation at the FBP1 Cys282 residue, catalyzed by zinc finger DHHC-type containing 13, further disrupted its gluconeogenic function, exacerbating lactate accumulation. To rescue these defects, we engineered lipid nanoparticles loaded with the Fbp1-C282S mutant mRNA, restoring FBP1 expression, blocking pathological palmitoylation, and ultimately improving erectile function in diabetic male mice. Here, our study in male mice identifies cavernosal lactate accumulation as a central pathological factor, elucidates its molecular regulation, and provide a targeted therapeutic strategy for DMED.

---

## Introduction

Erectile dysfunction (ED), defined as the persistent inability to attain or sustain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance, represents a common clinical condition that significantly diminishes quality of life and psychological well-being1. Diabetes mellitus is a major risk factor for ED, with diabetes mellitus-induced erectile dysfunction (DMED) exhibiting a prevalence ranging from 35.8 to 86.1% across diverse populations2,3. Compared to ED in non-diabetic individuals, DMED is characterized by earlier onset, more severe symptoms, and markedly reduced responsiveness to conventional therapies, presenting a substantial clinical management challenge4,5. While the pathogenesis of DMED involves a variety of cellular alterations and mediating factors, the precise mechanisms remain unclear.

Within the penile microenvironment, corpus cavernosum smooth muscle cells (CCSMCs) serve as the terminal effector regulating vascular tone and hemodynamics during erection6. Under diabetic conditions, CCSMCs sustain structural and functional damage through mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysregulation7, while concurrently undergoing a contractile-to-synthetic phenotypic transition that drives excessive extracellular matrix deposition and cavernosal fibrosis8. Consequently, preserving CCSMC integrity and function has emerged as a plausible therapeutic strategy for DMED, although the precise regulatory mechanisms governing these cells demand further investigation.

Lactate, once considered merely a metabolic waste product, is now recognized as a key signaling molecule with pleiotropic roles in cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, inflammatory, and oncological pathologies9. Elevated circulating lactate levels in diabetic patients—detectable even during prediabetic stages—correlate with early diabetes-associated complications10,11. Interestingly, sildenafil citrate, a first-line ED pharmacotherapy, was recently shown to reduce lactate accumulation in muscle following strenuous exercise and improve exercise performance in rats12. Gluconeogenesis maintains a critical homeostatic relationship with lactate metabolism. Under physiological conditions, lactate generated via glycolysis during hypoxia or high metabolic demand is reconverted to glucose through gluconeogenesis in the Cori cycle. Conversely, impaired gluconeogenesis disrupts this recycling axis, driving pathological lactate accumulation in susceptible tissues. Within this gluconeogenic pathway, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (FBP1) serves as a critical regulatory node governing lactate-to-glucose conversion. In cancers, FBP1 downregulation drives lactate-driven Warburg effect amplification, accelerating tumor invasion and metastasis13. In non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, suppressed FBP1 induces hepatic lactate buildup, exacerbating inflammation and steatosis14.

Here, we show that pathological cavernosal lactate accumulation drives DMED through structural degeneration and CCSMC loss. Transcriptional repression and functional impairment of Fbp1 constitute the core mechanism underlying lactate dysregulation, mediated by histone methylation and palmitoylation modifications. Critically, nanoparticle delivery of a palmitoylation-resistant Fbp1 mutant mRNA restores gluconeogenic flux, normalizes lactate levels, and rescues erectile function in diabetic mice. This work establishes aberrant lactate metabolism as a pathogenic cornerstone of DMED and proposes a metabolic reprogramming therapy.

---

## Results

Supplemental lactate impairs the CCSMC function and leads to DMED
After obtaining clinical ethics approval (LYEC2025-0188), we conducted an observational case-control study and recruited 60 patients with DMED—33 with mild, 19 with moderate, and 8 with severe ED—and 60 age-matched controls (Fig. 1a, b and Supplementary Fig. 1a). DMED patients exhibited significantly higher serum lactate and blood glucose levels compared to controls (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 1b). When all 120 participants were stratified into tertiles based on serum lactate levels, the overall incidence of ED increased significantly with ascending lactate tertiles (Fig. 1d). Moreover, within the DMED subgroup, the incidence of moderate-to-severe ED rose in a lactate-dependent manner (Fig. 1e).

To further investigate the correlation between lactate and DMED, we established a mouse model of DMED using a combination of low-dose streptozotocin and a high-fat diet. Cavernosal lactate concentrations and intracavernous pressure (ICP) were measured at 0, 4, 8, and 12 weeks post-modeling (Supplementary Fig. 1c). We observed a time-dependent increase in cavernosal lactate levels, accompanied by a progressive decline in ICP (Supplementary Fig. 1d–f). DMED mice also exhibited significantly elevated plasma lactate and blood glucose levels compared to controls (Supplementary Fig. 1g, h). Furthermore, cavernosal tissue in DMED mice showed pronounced lactate accumulation, with its levels positively correlating with plasma lactate concentrations (Fig. 1f–h).

To evaluate the effect of lactate on erectile function, mice were randomly assigned to receive saline or different doses of lactate (Fig. 1i). Serum lactate kinetics analysis showed that the 0.5 g/kg dose significantly elevated the concentration-time curve compared to the 0.25 g/kg group, whereas the 0.75 g/kg dose did not further increase lactate levels within the short term (Supplementary Fig. 1i). Therefore, the 0.25 and 0.5 g/kg doses were selected for subsequent experiments. Exogenous lactate administration elevated cavernosal lactate levels and reduced ICP in a concentration-dependent manner compared with the saline group (Fig. 1j–l). Histological analysis further revealed that lactate treatment significantly reduced the lumen-to-parenchyma ratio, smooth muscle-to-collagen ratio, and α-SMA fluorescence intensity, while increasing Collagen I fluorescence intensity (Fig. 1m–r and Supplementary Fig. 1j, k). These results demonstrate that elevated lactate levels disrupt erectile function by reducing smooth muscle content.

Based on the above findings, we further investigated the toxic effects of lactate accumulation on CCSMCs. Primary CCSMCs were treated with lactate at different concentrations (0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 mmol/L). Cell viability was not significantly affected at lactate concentrations up to and including 4 mmol/L (Supplementary Fig. 1l). Thus, 5 and 10 mmol/L were selected as low and high lactate stimulation concentrations, respectively, for subsequent experiments (Fig. 1s). Lactate treatment impaired CCSMCs’ activity and motility in a concentration-dependent manner (Fig. 1t–v). Western blot analysis showed that exposure to high lactate levels downregulated contractile markers (SM22α and CALPONIN) and upregulated synthetic markers (VIMENTIN and OSTEOPONTIN) in CCSMCs (Fig. 1w, x). Transcriptome sequencing further suggested that excessive autophagy activation may underlie the lactate-induced impairment of CCSMCs (Supplementary Fig. 2a–c). In vitro experiments were conducted by pretreating CCSMCs with the autophagy inhibitor 3-methyladenine (3-MA). The results demonstrated that 3-MA significantly abrogates lactate-induced excessive autophagy activation, impairment of cell viability, and phenotypic switching toward the synthetic smooth muscle phenotype. (Supplementary Fig. 2d–l). In animal models, we further analyzed autophagic activity in the corpus cavernosum of lactate-challenged mice and DMED mice. Intriguingly, progressive elevation of the LC3-II/LC3-I ratio was observed in both models during disease progression, whereas P62 protein expression exhibited a dynamic change characterized by an initial decrease followed by a subsequent increase (Supplementary Fig. 3). Building upon these observations, we performed interventions with 3-MA and SMER28, respectively. Our data showed that 3-MA effectively suppressed excessive autophagy and remarkably improved erectile function as well as tissue architecture in DMED mice. In contrast, although SMER28 promoted P62 degradation, it failed to exert significant therapeutic efficacy (Supplementary Fig. 4). Collectively, these results indicate that lactate-induced excessive autophagy is a key mechanism contributing to DMED.

FBP1 is a key factor for cavernosal lactate accumulation in DMED
Lactate serves as a key intermediate in glucose metabolism. Under anaerobic conditions, glycolysis rapidly converts glucose to lactate, while gluconeogenesis reversibly converts lactate back to glucose to maintain systemic glucose homeostasis (Fig. 2a). Consequently, tissue lactate accumulation can arise from either glycolytic overactivation, which leads to excessive lactate production, or impaired gluconeogenesis, which results in inadequate lactate clearance15. We have validated that CCSMC also possesses gluconeogenic function, consistent with what has been observed in smooth muscle cells from other sites16,17 (Supplementary Fig. 5). Using RNA-seq data from our previously established DMED mouse and rat models18, we analyzed the transcription profiles of key genes involved in glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. The results revealed no upregulation of glycolytic pathway genes. Furthermore, a brief exploratory treatment of DMED mice with sodium oxamate, a glycolysis inhibitor, did not significantly reduce cavernosal lactate levels (Supplementary Fig. 6a–c), suggesting that lactate accumulation in the corpus cavernosum primarily results from defective gluconeogenesis rather than enhanced glycolysis. Among gluconeogenic enzymes, Fbp1 showed consistent transcriptional downregulation (Fig. 2b, c). Analysis of public single-cell sequencing data from the Human Male Health Atlas (http://malehealthatlas.cn/)19 also indicated reduced FBP1 expression in the corpus cavernosum of DMED patients (Fig. 2d). Consistent with this, validation in DMED mouse models confirmed significant downregulation of FBP1, whereas the expression of G6PC3 and PCK1 remained unchanged (Fig. 2e–g and Supplementary Fig. 6d–f).

FBP1 catalyzes the hydrolysis of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into fructose 6-phosphate and inorganic phosphate, playing a critical role in lactate metabolism20. Its deficiency is associated with metabolic disturbances, including hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis21. We therefore asked whether FBP1 downregulation contributes to the development of ED. Our results demonstrated that Fbp1 knockdown significantly increased cavernosal lactate levels and reduced ICP, lumen-to-parenchyma ratio, and α-SMA fluorescence intensity compared to normal mice (Fig. 2h–n). Under low-lactate conditions in vitro, Fbp1 knockout further impaired CCSMC viability, motility, and contractile marker expression (Fig. 2o–q). Conversely, Fbp1 overexpression partially counteracted the detrimental effects of high lactate concentrations on CCSMCs (Fig. 2r–t). Notably, the G260R variant (the glycine at position 260 of the FBP1 is substituted with arginine), a well-characterized enzymatically inactive form of FBP1 linked to metabolic disorders22,23, was found in our study to fail in alleviating the harmful effects of high lactate concentrations on CCSMCs (Fig. 2r–t). These findings indicate that FBP1 modulates lactate-induced effects on CCSMCs in an enzyme activity-dependent manner.

Aberrant accumulation of H3K9me3 or H3K27me3 in the Fbp1 promoter epigenetically represses its transcription in DMED
Transcriptional regulation represents a fundamental mechanism controlling gene expression. As previously described, the transcriptional downregulation of Fbp1 was observed across species in penile cavernosal tissues. Given that histone methylation modifications can induce epigenetic repression of gene expression by altering chromatin structure, and have been implicated in various diabetic complications24–26, we hypothesized that these marks might contribute to Fbp1 silencing. To identify potential repressive histone modifications on the Fbp1 promoter, we performed an initial screening using the ChIP-Atlas database (https://chip-atlas.org/). The analysis revealed significant enrichment of the repressive marks histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3)27 and histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3)28 within the Fbp1 promoter region (Fig. 3a). We further validated these findings through ChIP-qPCR assays, which confirmed strong enrichment of both H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 at the Fbp1 promoter in MOVAS cells and primary mouse CCSMCs, and also characterized additional epigenetic features of the Fbp1 promoter (Fig. 3b, c and Supplementary Fig. 7a–g). Furthermore, we demonstrated that the enrichment of H3K9me3 or H3K27me3 were significantly elevated in the corpus cavernosum of DMED mice compared to normal mice (Fig. 3d, e). Since histone methylation is catalyzed by specific methyltransferases, we screened for enzymes associated with H3K9me3 and H3K27me3. This revealed substantial upregulation of suppressor of variegation 3-9 homolog 1 (SUV39H1) and enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) in DMED mice (Fig. 3f, g). Overexpression of Suv39h1 increased H3K9me3 levels and inhibited the FBP1 expression in both MOVAS cells (Fig. 3h, i) and CCSMCs (Supplementary Fig. 7h–i). Conversely, Suv39h1 knockdown using siRNA or inhibition with its specific inhibitor chaetocin29 led to the upregulation of FBP1 (Fig. 3j–m and Supplementary Fig. 7j–m). Similarly, Ezh2 overexpression elevated H3K27me3 and repressed FBP1, whereas Ezh2 knockdown or inhibition with EPZ643830 increased FBP1 expression (Supplementary Figs. 7n–s and 8). Given that the EZH2–H3K27me3 axis has been previously implicated in FBP1 regulation31–33, we focused on identifying readers of H3K9me3 at the Fbp1 promoter. Integrated analysis using ChIP-Atlas and ChIP-qPCR identified chromobox protein homolog 3 (CBX3), a known reader of H3K9me334, binding to the Fbp1 promoter (Fig. 3n, o and Supplementary Fig. 7t). CBX3 enrichment was significantly higher in DMED mice compared to normal mice (Fig. 3p, q). We further demonstrated that CBX3 negatively regulates FBP1 expression in vitro (Fig. 3r–y and Supplementary Fig. 7u–z), and to mechanistically target this regulation, we employed PROTAC technology35 to develop a selective CBX3 degrader that induces its ubiquitination-mediated degradation (Supplementary Fig. 9). Collectively, these findings indicate that aberrant enrichment of H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 at the Fbp1 promoter epigenetically represses its transcription in DMED.

The effects of H3K9me3- and H3K27me3-related inhibitors on DMED mice
Next, we evaluated the effects of the three inhibitors on Fbp1 function by measuring glucose consumption and lactate production. Treatment with inhibitors or siRNA targeting Cbx3, Suv39h1, or Ezh2 significantly reduced both glucose consumption and lactate production in cultured cells. However, with the exception of siCbx3 (Fig. 4b), most inhibitors failed to reverse the metabolic alterations caused by Fbp1 knockout, as reflected in lactate production and glucose uptake (Fig. 4a–l). Moreover, inhibition of Cbx3, Suv39h1, or Ezh2 did not restore Fbp1 expression in Fbp1-knockout cells (Fig. 4m–o and Supplementary Fig. 10a–c). These results indicate that Fbp1 acts as a key downstream effector of Cbx3, Suv39h1, and Ezh2, although Cbx3 and Suv39h1 may also modulate lactate and glucose metabolism through additional pathways. Subsequently, we administered H-PROTAC, chaetocin, and EPZ6438 to DMED mice and Fbp1−/+ mice, respectively. Although the three inhibitors elicited statistically significant effects in DMED mice, the improvements were modest: they led to only a slight reduction in cavernosal lactate levels and partial recovery of ICP, tissue morphology, and smooth muscle content. Notably, none of the inhibitors produced any beneficial effect in Fbp1−/+ mice (Fig. 4p–u). Although combined inhibition of both marks led to stronger Fbp1 upregulation in vitro (Supplementary Fig. 10d, e), the combined in vivo administration of the three agents—chaetocin (intraperitoneally), EPZ6438 (orally), and H-PROTAC (intracavernously)—was poorly tolerated in DMED mice. Therefore, rather than pursuing complex combination regimens, it is more compelling to explore alternative mechanisms governing FBP1 expression and function.

ZDHHC13 mediated S-palmitoylation of FBP1 at C282 site
The above findings indicate that although histone methylation modifications strongly suppress Fbp1 transcription in DMED, interventions targeting these epigenetic regulators failed to robustly restore erectile function in vivo. This discrepancy led us to reevaluate the regulatory landscape of FBP1 and hypothesize that its activity might be further modulated by post-translational modifications (PTMs). Given the critical role of the G260 residue in FBP1 enzymatic function and gluconeogenesis, we focused on identifying potential PTMs near this key site. Analysis of all PTMs within ±25 amino acids around the G260 of FBP1 has shown that, apart from the previously reported acetylation at K26936 and phosphorylation at Y26537, a palmitoylation site at C282 has been identified by using the CSS-palm 4.0 tool (Fig. 5a). Palmitoylation of FBP1 was confirmed via acyl-biotinyl exchange (ABE) assay in cells expressing HA-tagged Fbp1, with streptavidin blotting revealing a clear palmitoylation signal (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 11a). This finding was further validated using biotin-alkyne labeling coupled with click chemistry, which showed increased palmitoylated proteins in Fbp1-transfected cells; hydroxylamine treatment abolished this signal, confirming its specificity (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 11b, c). We also demonstrated that endogenous FBP1 undergoes palmitoylation (Supplementary Fig. 11d). Sequence alignment revealed that C282, located adjacent to the functional G260 residue, is evolutionarily conserved across species (Fig. 5d). To identify the enzyme responsible for FBP1 palmitoylation, we generated a series of Zdhhc knockout cell lines using CRISPR technology. Among these, knockout of zinc finger DHHC-type containing 13 (Zdhhc13) markedly reduced FBP1 palmitoylation (Fig. 5e), suggesting it acts as a key palmitoyltransferase for FBP1. The direct physical interaction between FBP1 and ZDHHC13 was further confirmed by molecular docking, co-immunoprecipitation, confocal imaging, and GST pull-down assays (Fig. 5f–j and Supplementary Fig. 11e). Transcriptome analysis and immunohistochemistry of the corpus cavernosum showed that ZDHHC13 expression was elevated in DMED mice (Fig. 5k, l), suggesting its involvement in FBP1 palmitoylation in vivo. In cellular models, knockdown of Zdhhc13 decreased FBP1 palmitoylation, whereas its overexpression increased palmitoylation levels (Fig. 5m, n and Supplementary Fig. 11f, g). Mutation of the cysteine at position 282 to serine (FBP1-C282S) abolished FBP1 palmitoylation (Fig. 5o and Supplementary Fig. 11h). To clarify the enzyme dependency, we reintroduced either wild-type ZDHHC13 (ZDHHC13-WT) or an enzymatically inactive mutant (ZDHHC13-C456S)38 into Zdhhc13-knockout cells. Only ZDHHC13-WT restored FBP1 palmitoylation, confirming the requirement for ZDHHC13 enzymatic activity (Fig. 5p and Supplementary Fig. 11i, j). To rule out interference from endogenous FBP1, we expressed FBP1‑WT or FBP1‑C282S in Fbp1-knockout cells. Exogenous FBP1‑WT underwent palmitoylation, whereas the FBP1‑C282S mutant did not (Fig. 5q and Supplementary Fig. 11k, l). Finally, the palmitoylation assay confirmed that ZDHHC13‑WT mediated palmitoylation of FBP1‑WT but not FBP1‑C282S, and ZDHHC13‑C456S failed to catalyze the modification (Fig. 5r). Together, these data demonstrate that ZDHHC13 catalyzes S-palmitoylation of FBP1 at cysteine 282.

ZDHHC13-mediated S-palmitoylation of FBP1 impairs its gluconeogenic function
S-palmitoylation is known to regulate protein stability, localization, and function39,40. To investigate how ZDHHC13-mediated S-palmitoylation influences FBP1, we initially assessed its effects on protein degradation and subcellular localization, but observed no significant changes in either (Fig. 6a, b). We then employed PyMOL to assess whether palmitoylation at C282 induces conformational changes in FBP1. Palmitoylation reduced the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) of the critical G260 residue by ~20% (from 3.296 to 2.657 Å²), while the total SASA of chain A decreased by ~388 Å² (Supplementary Fig. 12a). Together, these data suggest that palmitoylation at C282 promotes a more compact conformational state of FBP1, characterized by reduced solvent exposure of G260 and enhanced local structural folding. Fbp1 knockout significantly elevated glucose consumption, lactate production, and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), while suppressing the oxygen consumption rate (OCR). Reintroduction of the Fbp1 C282S mutant into Fbp1‑knockout cells produced a greater reduction in glucose consumption, lactate production, and ECAR, alongside a more substantial increase in OCR (Fig. 6c–f and Supplementary Fig. 12b–g). Knockdown of Zdhhc13 significantly decreased glucose consumption, lactate production, and ECAR, and increased OCR. However, these metabolic changes were abolished in Fbp1-knockout cells (Fig. 6g–j and Supplementary Fig. 12h–k). Conversely, overexpression of Zdhhc13 increased glucose consumption, lactate production, and ECAR, while decreasing OCR; again, these effects were absent in Fbp1-knockout cells (Fig. 6k–n and Supplementary Fig. 12l–o). The enzymatically inactive mutant Zdhhc13-C456S had no significant effect on glycolytic activity or lactate production (Supplementary Fig. 12p–w). Furthermore, in Fbp1-knockout cells reconstituted with the Fbp1C282S mutant, Zdhhc13 overexpression failed to alter glucose consumption or lactate production (Supplementary Fig. 12x, y). Finally, we injected an adeno-associated virus (AAV) encoding Zdhhc13-targeting shRNA into the corpus cavernosum of DMED mice and Fbp1−/+ mice, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 12z). Knockdown of Zdhhc13 partially reduced cavernosal lactate levels and moderately improved ICP in DMED mice; however, it produced no effect in Fbp1−/+ mice (Fig. 6o–t). These results underscore that targeting Zdhhc13 alone provides limited therapeutic benefit in DMED. Building on these limitations, we next sought to elucidate the mechanism underlying Zdhhc13 upregulation in DMED. We analyzed differentially expressed genes using KEGG pathway enrichment, which revealed significant activation of the PI3K-AKT pathway—the most upregulated signaling pathway in DMED (Supplementary Fig. 13a). Given established knowledge of PI3K-AKT signaling in regulating SRY-related HMG-box gene 9 (SOX9) activity41,42, we investigated this potential connection. Interestingly, ChIP-Atlas data indicated SOX9 binding to the promoters of both Zdhhc13 and Cbx3 (Supplementary Fig. 13b). Consistent with these findings, we confirmed elevated phosphorylated AKT and SOX9 levels in the cavernosum of DMED mice (Supplementary Fig. 13c). Sox9 knockdown downregulated CBX3 and ZDHHC13 expression, while its overexpression increased them (Supplementary Fig. 13d–i). However, when we administered AAV-shSox9 to the cavernosum of DMED mice, we observed no significant improvement in cavernosal lactate levels or ICP (Supplementary Fig. 13j–m). This unexpected outcome prompted us to explore alternative strategies capable of concurrently addressing both Fbp1 transcriptional repression and palmitoylative inactivation.

The effect of lipid nanoparticles loaded with Fbp1-C282S mRNA on DMED mice
Currently, single-site inhibitors demonstrate only modest efficacy in vivo, failing to substantially ameliorate elevated lactate levels or restore erectile function in DMED mice. Furthermore, combination therapy with multiple agents may provoke serious adverse reactions. To address this challenge, we synthesized the Fbp1-C282S mRNA using site-directed mutagenesis, which was subsequently encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (Fbp1-C282S-LNP) via the Ignite Nano Assay system (Fig. 7a). The Fbp1-C282S-LNPs exhibited an average particle size of 99.3 nm, polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.083, encapsulation efficiency of 90.8%, and zeta potential of −3.44 mV (Fig. 7b). Scanning electron microscopy was used to further characterize the nanoparticles (Fig. 7c). The Fbp1-C282S-LNPs significantly upregulated FBP1 level without exhibiting obvious cytotoxicity in primary mouse CCSMCs (Fig. 7d–f). Functional assays confirmed that the Fbp1-C282S-LNPs also markedly downregulated glucose consumption, lactate production and ECAR, while upregulating cellular OCR (Fig. 7g–n). Subsequently, we encapsulated Flag-tagged Fbp1-C282S mRNA into LNPs and evaluated cellular uptake within the corpus cavernosum using multiplex immunofluorescence staining. Robust LNPs uptake was observed in CCSMCs, with detectable internalization also occurring in endothelial cells and fibroblasts (Supplementary Fig. 14a). Additionally, in vivo assessments confirmed this formulation induced no significant hepatic or renal toxicity in mice (Supplementary Fig. 14b–e). Concurrently, we completed pharmacokinetic and tissue distribution studies of Fbp1-C282S-LNPs to define their in vivo profiles (Supplementary Fig. 14f, g). To assess dose-dependent therapeutic efficacy, DMED mice received intracavernous injections of Fbp1-C282S-LNPs at 0.1, 0.25, or 0.5 mg/kg. The 0.1 mg/kg group showed no significant improvement in cavernosal lactate levels or erectile function relative to controls. In contrast, the 0.25 mg/kg group significantly reduced lactate levels, increased FBP1 expression, improved ICP, enhanced smooth muscle content, ameliorated histological structure, and reduced cavernous fibrosis. However, the 0.5 mg/kg group provided no additional therapeutic benefit over the 0.25 mg/kg dose (Fig. 7o–y). We validated that Fbp1 C282S-LNP treatment can also efficiently reverse autophagic abnormalities in the corpus cavernosum of DMED mice (Supplementary Fig. 14h-j). Results of subsequent multi-tissue validation demonstrated that, in contrast to the significant increase in FBP1 protein expression observed in the corpus cavernosum following treatment, FBP1 protein expression in the liver and skeletal muscle exhibited an upward trend but failed to reach statistical significance (Supplementary Fig. 15). Furthermore, Fbp1-C282S-LNPs demonstrated sustained efficacy in long-term studies of DMED mice (Supplementary Fig. 16) and consistently improved outcomes across multiple diabetic models, including type 1 diabetes (Supplementary Fig. 17), db/db mice (Supplementary Fig. 18), and Fbp1−/+ mice (Supplementary Fig. 19). These results firmly establish Fbp1-C282S-LNP as a highly promising therapeutic strategy for DMED.
