function, especially Zdhhc13 promoted palmitoylation of Fbp1 through its
acyltransferase activity, thereby impairing cell function. Although inhibition of Fbp1
acylation or histone methylation failed to completely restore erectile function in
DMED mice, the development of a Fbp1-C282S mRNA-encapsulated lipid
nanoparticle (LNP) treatment regimen successfully reduced lactate levels and
significantly improved erectile function in the DMED mouse model, showing new
therapeutic prospects. Finally, the study pointed out that there is still room for
optimization of this treatment strategy, and the possibility of more drug combination
therapy should be explored in the future. It has a scientific value in this field. But
there are still some issues and questions that need to be addressed. Lacks of study in
human erectile tissues (this is very important because, as far as I know, there is no
study showing the relationship between lactate and ED in human erectile tissue) and
absence of data related to other important cellular components of erectile tissue, such
as endothelial cells, pericytes, and neuronal cells, are a major limitation of this study.
1. Was there a specific time-point of lactate accumulation in the corpus
cavernosum during the progression of DMED?
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer for raising this important question
regarding the temporal dynamics of lactate accumulation in corpus cavernosum—a
core aspect our study aimed to elucidate. Your insightful comment has provided
valuable guidance for improving the presentation of our results.
In direct response to your inquiry, our experimental design specifically incorporated
longitudinal assessments to capture the dynamic process of cavernosal lactate
accumulation. Using an established Type 2 DMED mouse model validated in previous
studies (e.g., PMID: 37217862; PMID: 37445656), we systematically measured
cavernosal lactate concentrations at four time points: baseline (Week 0), Week 4,
Week 8, and Week 12 post-modeling. Our results demonstrated a progressive,
time-dependent increase in cavernosal lactate accumulation, which correlated
inversely with declining intracavernosal pressure. These data are now clearly
presented in Supplementary Figure 1 and described in the revised Results section 1.
We have revised the manuscript to more explicitly highlight the temporal relationship
between metabolic changes and functional impairment in DMED progression. Thank
you again for this constructive suggestion, which has significantly strengthened our
data presentation.
2. Lactate supplementation: How do the doses of lactate given (0.25 g/kg/d and
0.5 g/kg/d) relate to physiological levels? Are these doses intended to mimic
pathological conditions? Are there data on how lactate affects healthy tissues?
How should the dose be chosen?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising these critical questions
regarding our lactate supplementation approach. Their comments have helped us
clarify the rationale behind our dose selection and improve the interpretation of our
results.
In response, we would like to explain that the lactate doses used (0.25 and 0.5 g/kg/d)
were specifically chosen to replicate pathological lactate levels observed in our
diabetic mouse model, rather than physiological conditions. Our data demonstrated
significantly elevated lactate concentrations in both serum and corpus cavernosum
tissue in diabetic mice, with a positive correlation between these compartments
(Figure1).
To determine the appropriate dosing regimen, we first consulted previous studies
involving lactate supplementation(PMID:38925041). We then conducted pilot
experiments testing three doses (0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 g/kg/d). Results revealed that 0.5
g/kg/d significantly increased the serum lactate exposure compared to the lower dose,
while the highest dose provided no further increase. Using our established correlation
between serum and cavernosal lactate levels, we found that 0.5 g/kg/d effectively
elevated cavernosal lactate to the pathological range observed in DMED mice. These
preliminary data supported the selection of the two doses(0.25 and 0.5 g/kg/d) for
formal experiments, as they allowed us to mimic pathological conditions while
avoiding potential non-specific effects at higher doses. These data are now clearly
presented in Supplementary Figure 1 and described in the revised Results section 1.
Subsequent experiments confirmed that exogenous lactate administration resulted in
dose-dependent impairments in erectile function in mice and corpus cavernosum
smooth muscle cells (Figure1).
We thank the reviewer again for these insightful questions, which have significantly
improved the rigor and clarity of our experimental design.
3. Clinical relevance of lactate measurements: While the study focuses on lactate
accumulation in the corpus cavernosum, how directly do these findings correlate
to human DMED? Are plasma lactate levels in DMED patients also elevated to
the same extent as observed in the mice?
Response: We sincerely appreciate your thoughtful questions regarding the clinical
relevance of lactate measurements. The issues you raised—specifically, the
association between corpus cavernosum lactate accumulation in mice and human
DMED, as well as the characteristics of lactate changes in DMED patients—are
central to validating the clinical significance of our study and crucial for strengthening
the translational value of our findings. Below, we provide a point-by-point response
integrating both clinical data and experimental details.
To directly address the relationship between corpus cavernosum lactate accumulation
in mice and human DMED, we first obtained approval from the Clinical Ethics
Committee (LYEC2025-0188). We then recruited 60 DMED patients—classified as
33 mild, 19 moderate, and 8 severe cases—along with 60 healthy controls, carefully
matching for confounders such as age. Serum lactate levels were systematically
measured in all participants. The results revealed significantly higher serum lactate
levels in DMED patients (2.4 mmol/L) compared to healthy controls (1.7 mmol/L; p =
0.0002). This observation of elevated lactate aligns with the increased lactate levels
observed both in serum and corpus cavernosum tissue in our DMED mouse model,
thereby offering clinical support for the role of lactate in the pathophysiology of
DMED.
It should be noted that due to ethical constraints and practical challenges in procuring
human corpus cavernosum tissue, direct measurement of local lactate concentrations
in DMED patients was not feasible. However, in our mouse model of DMED, we
identified a significant positive linear correlation between plasma lactate and corpus
cavernosum lactate levels. This correlation provides an important basis for inferring
that local lactate concentrations within the corpus cavernosum of DMED patients may
also be elevated, further supporting the translational relevance of our animal findings
to human disease.
To further assess the clinical association between lactate levels and DMED, we
stratified all 120 participants into three tertiles based on serum lactate levels: lower
third (<1/3), middle third (1/3–2/3), and upper third (>2/3). In the overall cohort, the
incidence of erectile dysfunction (ED) exhibited a significant increasing trend across
rising lactate tertiles (p=0.002). The incidence of ED in the upper third was
significantly higher than that in the lower third (p=0.001; Cramer’s V = 0.376).
Post-hoc pairwise comparisons were performed using the chi-square partition method
with a corrected significance level of α' = 0.017.
Among DMED patients specifically, the incidence of moderate-to-severe ED also rose
with increasing lactate levels (p=0.014). Notably, the rate of severe ED was
significantly higher in patients within the upper lactate tertile compared to those in the
lower tertile (p=0.004; Cramer’s V=0.376). These results not only reinforce the
association between elevated lactate and DMED but also demonstrate a dose-response
relationship wherein higher lactate levels correlate with greater disease severity,
thereby enhancing the clinical applicability of our conclusions.
In summary, our clinical data support the involvement of lactate in DMED
pathophysiology through several lines of evidence: consistency between animal and
human lactate trends, stratification analysis confirming a dose-dependent relationship,
and extrapolation from plasma-cavernosal lactate correlation in mice—compensating
for the inability to directly measure human tissue lactate. These aspects have been
incorporated into Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 1 of the revised manuscript.
We are truly grateful for your insightful comments, which have prompted us to more
clearly articulate the clinical implications of our work and further improve the rigor
and persuasiveness of our conclusions.
4. Role of Zdhhc13-mediated palmitoylation: The role of Zdhhc13 in Fbp1
palmitoylation and its subsequent impact on gluconeogenesis is intriguing. Could
the manuscript expand on the mechanism by which palmitoylation at C282
disrupts Fbp1 function? Is there a pathway implicated in the degradation or
inactivation of Fbp1 upon palmitoylation?
Response:
We sincerely appreciate your valuable comments regarding the mechanism by which
C282 palmitoylation disrupts Fbp1 function, as well as the potential involvement of
degradation or inactivation pathways. Your questions are essential for further
elucidating the molecular mechanism of Zdhhc13-mediated palmitoylation. Based on
our experimental data, we have organized the following response:
Fbp1 is a rate-limiting enzyme in lactate metabolism. Previous studies have
established that residue G260 within its catalytic site is critical for enzymatic
activity—any disruption at this site impairs Fbp1 function and leads to lactate
accumulation (PMID: 20151204, 28720574). In this study, multiple experimental
approaches, including glucose consumption, lactate production, and Seahorse
extracellular flux analyses, consistently demonstrated that Zdhhc13-mediated
palmitoylation at C282 significantly impairs the gluconeogenic function of Fbp1
(Figures 6). To investigate the mechanism, we first excluded potential effects on
protein stability and subcellular localization, as palmitoylation at C282 did not alter
Fbp1 degradation or localization (Figures 6A–6B). We therefore proposed that
structural perturbation may underlie the loss of function.
Simulation of palmitoylated Fbp1 using PyMOL revealed that modification at C282
reduces the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) of the catalytic residue G260 by
approximately 20% (from 3.296 Å² to 2.657 Å²), while the total SASA of chain A
decreased by approximately 388 Å² (Supplementary Figure 8A). These results suggest
that palmitoylation induces a more compact conformation in Fbp1, which reduces the
solvent exposure of G260 and enhances local structural folding. Since G260 is
essential for catalytic activity, its impaired accessibility likely hinders substrate or
cofactor binding, thereby disrupting enzymatic function and gluconeogenesis.
In summary, our findings indicate that Zdhhc13-mediated palmitoylation of Fbp1 at
C282 induces conformational compaction, reduces solvent accessibility of the
catalytic residue G260, and thereby inhibits Fbp1 enzymatic activity and
gluconeogenic function—independent of changes in protein degradation or
localization. We thank you once again for your thorough and insightful questions,
which have helped us better articulate the mechanistic details of this regulatory
pathway.
5. Therapeutic potential of Fbp1 rescue: Fbp1 C282S-loaded lipid nanoparticles
(Fbp1 C282S-LNP) are proposed as a potential therapeutic strategy. Can the
manuscript include more detailed pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic data
on the efficacy of these nanoparticles in vivo, including potential off-target
effects?
Response: We sincerely appreciate your critical questions concerning the therapeutic
potential of Fbp1 C282S-loaded lipid nanoparticles (Fbp1 C282S-LNPs). In response
to your inquiries regarding in vivo pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, tissue
distribution, cellular uptake, and potential off-target effects, we have summarized the
key experimental findings below:
To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of Fbp1 C282S-LNPs, we administered
intracavernous injections to DMED mice at three dose levels (0.1 mg/kg, 0.25 mg/kg,
and 0.5 mg/kg), along with a control group. The results indicated that the 0.1 mg/kg
dose did not effectively reduce lactate levels in the corpus cavernosum or improve
erectile function. In contrast, the 0.25 mg/kg dose significantly decreased lactate
accumulation and enhanced erectile performance. The 0.5 mg/kg dose did not yield
statistically superior efficacy compared to the 0.25 mg/kg group, suggesting that 0.25
mg/kg is an effective dose approaching pharmacodynamic saturation.
Multiplex immunofluorescence staining (using Flag tag for Fbp1 C282S-LNPs, and
markers for endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and fibroblasts: vWF, α-SMA, and
vimentin, respectively) revealed strong LNP uptake in smooth muscle cells, with
detectable internalization in endothelial cells and fibroblasts. This indicates that the
LNPs can target multiple relevant cell types within the penile tissue.
Further pharmacokinetic analysis via LC-MS/MS of orbital blood samples showed
that Fbp1 C282S-LNPs have an elimination half-life of 12.57±1.51 hours. To assess
tissue distribution and potential off-target effects, DiD-labeled LNPs were used: the
highest fluorescence intensity was observed in the corpus cavernosum at 0.25 hours
post-injection, followed by a gradual decline, confirming rapid target tissue
accumulation and sustained local concentration. In the liver—the primary clearance
organ—fluorescence intensity initially increased and then decreased without abnormal
retention. Only minimal fluorescence was detected in skeletal muscle and the spleen,
and due to the blood-brain barrier, brain fluorescence remained negligible throughout,
effectively ruling out central nervous system exposure. Additionally, measurements of
liver and kidney function markers (ALT, AST, serum creatinine, and blood urea
nitrogen) showed no significant differences between treated and control groups,
supporting the absence of hepatorenal toxicity.
It is worth emphasizing that although LNPs were taken up by both penile and
non-penile tissues (such as liver and skeletal muscle), we believe this “non-strict
targeting” profile enhances rather than diminishes therapeutic efficacy through two
complementary mechanisms: uptake in liver and muscle enhances systemic lactate
metabolism, thereby reducing lactate delivery to the corpus cavernosum; meanwhile,
uptake within penile endothelial cells and fibroblasts contributes to local lactate
consumption. Thus, the broad targeting capability of LNPs supports a synergistic
therapeutic strategy combining local and systemic effects, with no significant adverse
effects observed.
All relevant data—including dose-response outcomes, pharmacokinetic parameters,
tissue distribution, cellular uptake, and safety assessments—have been added as
Figure 7 and Supplementary Figure 10 in the revised manuscript. These results
collectively support the therapeutic potential and safety of Fbp1 C282S-LNPs. We are
truly grateful for your thorough and insightful comments, which have helped us
present these findings more comprehensively and strengthen the overall rigor of our
study.
6. Histological analysis: More specific histological analysis (e.g.,
immunohistochemistry or immunofluorescence) could help validate the effects of
lactate on smooth muscle function and fibrosis. Were markers of fibrosis (e.g.,
collagen type I) assessed in the cavernosal tissue?
Response: We sincerely appreciate your valuable suggestions regarding the
histological analysis. Your focus on validating the effects of lactate on cavernous
smooth muscle function and fibrosis—particularly through immunohistochemistry or
immunofluorescence targeting markers such as collagen type I—has provided
essential guidance for strengthening the evidence linking lactate to pathological
changes in the corpus cavernosum. Based on your comments, we have conducted
additional experiments and integrated the findings as follows:
To further investigate the role of lactate in cavernous fibrosis, we performed
immunofluorescence staining for collagen type I. The results demonstrated a positive
correlation between the concentration of intraperitoneally injected sodium lactate and
the fluorescence intensity of collagen type I within cavernous tissue. This outcome
aligns with the fibrotic features previously observed via hematoxylin-eosin (HE)
staining and Masson’s trichrome staining, together providing compelling evidence
that elevated lactate levels promote cavernous fibrosis.
Furthermore, we expanded the scope of our investigation to include type 1 diabetes,
type 2 diabetes, and db/db mouse models (a spontaneous type 2 diabetes model).
In these models, we supplemented the evaluation with assessments of collagen type I
expression in cavernous tissue following treatment with Fbp1 C282S-LNPs. This
additional analysis aims to more comprehensively evaluate the therapeutic potential of
this strategy in alleviating lactate-mediated cavernous fibrosis.
We are truly grateful for your thorough and insightful suggestions, which have guided
us to deepen our investigation into the relationship between lactate and cavernous
tissue damage at the level of fibrosis markers. Your comments have significantly
enhanced the scientific soundness and rigor of our conclusions. All results from these
supplementary experiments have been included in the revised manuscript.
7. Comparative analysis of other gluconeogenic enzymes: Given the role of Fbp1
in gluconeogenesis, it might be beneficial to compare the expression of other key
gluconeogenic enzymes (such as G6PC, PCK1) in the corpus cavernosum of
DMED mice to ensure that the observed effects are Fbp1-specific and not part of
a broader metabolic dysfunction.
Response: Thank you for suggesting the comparison with other key gluconeogenic
enzymes (e.g., G6PC and PCK1), which helps confirm the specific role of Fbp1—
rather than general metabolic dysfunction—in lactate accumulation in the corpus
cavernosum of DMED mice. We have conducted further investigations using
transcriptomic data and validation experiments, and provide the following response:
Glucose can be rapidly metabolized to lactate via glycolysis, while lactate can be
reconverted to glucose through gluconeogenesis to help maintain systemic glucose
homeostasis. Tissue lactate accumulation typically arises from one of two scenarios:
excessive glycolytic activation leading to increased lactate production, or impaired
gluconeogenesis resulting in reduced lactate consumption. To identify the primary
cause of lactate accumulation in our DMED model, we analyzed RNA-seq data from
both mouse and rat DMED models, focusing on key enzymes in glycolysis and
gluconeogenesis. The results indicated that glycolytic enzymes were broadly
suppressed, suggesting that lactate accumulation in the corpus cavernosum is more
likely due to impaired lactate consumption—specifically, deficient gluconeogenic
function.
Supporting this hypothesis, transcriptomic analysis in both species revealed
significant downregulation of Fbp1 at the mRNA level. Subsequent validation in
DMED mice confirmed that Fbp1 expression was markedly reduced at both the
transcriptional and protein levels. In contrast, the other two key gluconeogenic
enzymes, G6pc3 and Pck1, showed inconsistent transcriptional changes across species
(e.g., G6pc3 was unchanged in mice but slightly upregulated in rats). Furthermore,
qPCR and protein-level assays in DMED mice confirmed that neither G6pc3 nor Pck1
exhibited significant alterations, effectively excluding their involvement in lactate
accumulation.
In summary, our findings indicate that lactate accumulation in the corpus cavernosum
of DMED mice results primarily from the specific downregulation and functional
impairment of Fbp1, rather than from a general disruption of gluconeogenic enzymes.
We thank you once again for your insightful suggestions, which have helped us more
precisely delineate the central role of Fbp1 in DMED pathology and strengthened the
specificity and reliability of our conclusions. The relevant data have been added to
Figure 2 and Supplementary Figure 2 in the revised manuscript.
8. The introduction could benefit from a clearer explanation of the significance of
Fbp1 in diabetic erectile dysfuncton(DMED). Why is Fbp1 a key player in the
pathophysiology of DMED? Why other targets, such as Hk2, Pklr, Pck1 were not
select? These targets expression pattern looks similar with Fbp1.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your insightful comments, which are
invaluable for refining the introduction and clarifying the central role of Fbp1 in
DMED. In response, we have provided a concise explanation based on our research
rationale and available evidence:
Although no studies have directly linked Fbp1 to ED, we have highlighted its
potential role in DMED in the revised introduction through two key aspects: (1) the
mechanistic connection between impaired gluconeogenesis and lactate accumulation,
and (2) the pathological relevance of Fbp1 deficiency-mediated lactate accumulation
in various diseases. As the rate-limiting enzyme of gluconeogenesis, dysregulation of
Fbp1 directly impedes lactate clearance via gluconeogenesis, thereby contributing to
related pathological damage.
Regarding the selection of targets such as Hk2, Pklr, and Pck1, we previously
provided a detailed response (Question 6), which can be summarized as follows: Hk2
and Pklr, both glycolytic enzymes that promote lactate production, were found to be
downregulated in transcriptomic data from mouse and rat models, suggesting they do
not drive lactate accumulation in DMED. Although Pck1 is involved in
gluconeogenesis, its expression remained unchanged in DMED mouse tissues. Thus,
these targets were not selected for further investigation.
We are truly grateful for your suggestions, which have greatly improved the focus and
logical soundness of our introduction and strengthened the foundation for presenting
our subsequent findings.
9. While Cbx3 is shown to interact with H3K9me3, what are its specific effects on
Fbp1 function in terms of cellular metabolism or other pathways? Could
metabolic assays help elucidate its role further?
Response: We sincerely appreciate your question, which insightfully addresses the
central relationship between Cbx3 and Fbp in metabolic regulation. Our experimental
results have clearly elucidated the underlying mechanisms and functional
consequences:
Specifically, we have demonstrated that Cbx3 transcriptionally regulates Fbp1.
Functional assays, including glucose consumption and lactate production
measurements, further confirm that Cbx3 modulates the gluconeogenic activity of
Fbp1 through this regulatory mechanism. The process can be summarized as follows:
upregulation of Cbx3 suppresses Fbp1 expression. Since Fbp1 serves as a key
rate-limiting enzyme in gluconeogenesis, its downregulation directly impairs
gluconeogenic function, leading to inadequate lactate consumption through this
metabolic pathway and consequent lactate accumulation.
Thank you once again for your valuable input. These validated findings provide
critical evidence clarifying the role of the “Cbx3–Fbp1–lactate metabolism” axis in
the pathological process.
10. Although Fbp1-C282S-LNP improves various functional parameters in
DMED mice, the manuscript could benefit from a more detailed discussion of
how this strategy compares to traditional therapeutic interventions for DMED.
Could this approach be combined with other treatment modalities?
Response: We sincerely thank you for your insightful comments, which have greatly
inspired our research. In response, we have added the following content to the
Discussion section to clarify the differences between Fbp1-C282S-LNP and
conventional DMED treatments, as well as their potential for combination therapy:
Phosphodiesterase 5 (PDE5) inhibitors, as first-line therapeutics for ED, act by
maintaining intracellular cGMP levels to promote smooth muscle relaxation and
enhance penile blood flow [PMID: 34183196]. However, it should be noted that
PDE5 inhibitors target only vasodilatory signaling pathways and do not address the
underlying structural damage to smooth muscle in DMED. Consequently, their
efficacy in DMED patients remains limited [PMID: 32257866; PMID: 22282735].
In contrast, Fbp1-C282S-LNP delivers therapeutic mRNA directly to the damaged
tissue, reducing local lactate accumulation, mitigating smooth muscle impairment,
and promoting functional recovery. This approach targets the “structural damage”
itself—a dimension beyond the reach of PDE5 inhibitors. The complementary
mechanisms of these two strategies suggest strong potential for combination therapy:
Fbp1-C282S-LNP restores tissue integrity, establishing a structural foundation for
functional recovery, while PDE5 inhibitors enhance vasodilatory signaling. Such
synergy may significantly improve treatment outcomes, particularly in patients with
resistance to PDE5 inhibitors.
We are truly grateful for your valuable suggestions, which have helped us more
clearly articulate the unique advantages of the Fbp1-C282S-LNP strategy, broaden our
perspective on combination therapy, and enhance the depth and clinical relevance of
the Discussion. Your feedback provides important guidance for refining our future
research directions.
11. Fbp1 knockout mice are used in several experiments; however, the role of
Fbp1 in other tissues or systemic effects (e.g., liver or muscle) should be
considered. Could the observed effects be specific to the corpus cavernosum or
systemic in nature?
Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful feedback, which has prompted us
to more thoroughly consider potential systemic effects within our study design. Based
on our current findings and limitations, we provide the following response:
Our study demonstrated that blood lactate levels were significantly elevated in DMED
patients compared to healthy controls. Preclinical data also showed increased lactate
concentrations in the corpus cavernosum of DMED mice, which correlated positively
with systemic lactate levels. The primary focus of our research was to elucidate the
effect of lactate on penile function and the mechanism underlying its local
accumulation in the corpus cavernosum. That said, we fully acknowledge the
limitations of our current work. First, The Fbp1-/+ mice used in this study are not
penile tissue-specific knockdown models. It has been reported in the literature that
Fbp1-/+ mice exhibit inhibited Fbp1 gene expression in multiple tissues/organs
[38834617]. Second, although intracavernous injection of Fbp1-C282S-LNP
improved local retention, some uptake was still detected in the liver and skeletal
muscle. Therefore, we cannot entirely exclude the possibility that lactate derived from
systemic sources (e.g., liver or muscle) may contribute to pathological changes in the
corpus cavernosum.
We are truly grateful for your valuable suggestions, which have encouraged deeper
reflection on the tissue specificity and systemic implications of our results. Your
comments not only help us present the limitations of this study more objectively but
also provide important guidance for future research—such as developing
tissue-specific knockdown models and improving the targeting efficiency of LNPs.
12. Lactate Accumulation and Erectile Dysfunction: The link between lactate
accumulation and erectile dysfunction is mentioned, but the underlying cellular
mechanisms are not fully explained. Could the authors elaborate on how lactate
directly impairs CCSMC and erectile function at the molecular or cellular level?
Response: We sincerely thank you for your valuable suggestion, which accurately
identifies a central gap in understanding the molecular link between lactate and
DMED. Your comment has provided essential guidance for further mechanistic
investigation.
To clarify the specific molecular mechanism by which lactate impairs CCSMCs, we
performed transcriptome sequencing on primary CCSMCs following lactate treatment.
Bioinformatics analysis revealed a marked activation of autophagy-related pathways
in lactate-exposed cells. Supported by subsequent in vitro validation and existing
literature [PMID:24307209], we propose that lactate may induce persistent
overactivation of autophagy, thereby compromising the structural and functional
integrity of CCSMCs. This ultimately leads to reduced cell viability and impaired
contractile–relaxation capacity. These findings provide clear molecular evidence
supporting a direct role of lactate in CCSMC damage, and the relevant data have been
included in Supplementary Figure 1.
We are truly grateful for your insightful input, which encouraged us to pursue
transcriptome-level mechanistic evidence. Your suggestion has not only strengthened
the logical chain connecting lactate, excessive autophagy, and CCSMC damage, but
also laid a foundation for further clinical validation of this pathway.
13. LNP-Based Therapy: The use of LNPs for delivering the Fbp1-C282S mRNA
is promising, but the manuscript would benefit from a deeper discussion of how
LNPs are taken up by specific cell types, particularly in cavernosal tissue. What
are the advantages of LNP delivery over other methods?
Response: We greatly appreciate your insightful question and valuable input.
In response, we have provided detailed explanations in Questions 5 and 10, and would
like to briefly summarize the key findings here: During in vivo distribution studies of
the LNPs, significant uptake was observed not only in cavernous tissue but also in
other organs. To further investigate the cellular specificity of LNP uptake within
penile tissue, we encapsulated Flag-tagged Fbp1-C282S mRNA into LNPs and
performed multiplex immunofluorescence staining. The results demonstrated LNP
uptake across major penile cell types—endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and
fibroblasts—with the highest efficiency observed in smooth muscle cells, followed by
detectable uptake in endothelial cells and fibroblasts.
Based on these findings, we propose that although smooth muscle cells display high
metabolic activity, lactate-induced pathological damage within the corpus cavernosum
is not confined to a single cell type. Moreover, enhanced gluconeogenic function in
endothelial cells and fibroblasts following LNP uptake may help reduce local lactate
levels, thereby mitigating lactate-mediated tissue injury.
We have also expanded the Discussion section to include a comparison between the
LNP delivery system and other treatment strategies (e.g., PDE5 inhibitors), along with
a detailed explanation of the potential for combination therapies.
Once again, we sincerely thank you for your thoughtful comments, which have helped
us present our experimental findings and therapeutic concepts more systematically
and convincingly.
14. Limitations in Cell-Type Specificity: The study focuses on the effect of Fbp1
on CCSMCs, but the corpus cavernosum contains various cell types. How might
Fbp1-C282S affect other cells like endothelial cells, fibroblasts, pericytes, or
macrophages? Would the delivery system need to target these cells specifically?
Response: We sincerely thank you for your insightful question regarding the
multi-cellular role within the corpus cavernosum and the delivery strategy of LNPs.
Your feedback has been invaluable in refining our interpretation. Our key findings are
summarized below:
Experimental results indicate that LNPs are taken up not only by CCSMCs, but also
by other penile cell types, including endothelial cells and fibroblasts, as well as by
systemic tissues such as the liver and skeletal muscle. As a rate-limiting enzyme in
gluconeogenesis, Fbp1-C282S delivered via LNPs enhances lactate metabolism both
within and outside the penile tissue. This action promotes the conversion of lactate to
glucose, thereby directly and indirectly modulating cavernous lactate levels.
Specifically, within non-smooth muscle cells of the penis, Fbp1-C282S may help
reduce lactate-induced cytotoxicity, improving the local pathological
microenvironment and supporting functional recovery. Systemically, enhanced lactate
metabolism in organs such as the liver and skeletal muscle may further contribute to
lowering lactate levels in the corpus cavernosum. The broad biodistribution of
non-targeted LNPs allows them to simultaneously engage multiple cell types and
tissues involved in lactate metabolism, resulting in a synergistic therapeutic effect.
Thus, rather than being a limitation, this non-specificity offers a therapeutic advantage
by avoiding metabolic “blind spots” that could arise from overly restrictive targeting.
We are truly grateful for your suggestions, which have helped us present a more
rigorous and coherent mechanism of action, emphasizing the benefits of multi-target
metabolic regulation.
15. In Vivo Validation of mRNA Strategy: While the Fbp1-C282S mRNA strategy
shows promising outcomes, did the authors observe any long-term effects or
changes in other metabolic pathways? How sustained are the improvements in
erectile function over time?
Response: We sincerely appreciate your valuable suggestions. This question
accurately points to the long-term efficacy and metabolic safety of the mRNA
therapeutic strategy, providing a key direction for us to improve the demonstration of
the clinical translational value of our research.
In previous experiments, we found that the 0.25 mg/kg dose significantly reduced
cavernous lactate levels in DMED mice, alleviated tissue fibrosis. To further evaluate
its long-term efficacy, we additionally set a 1-month drug withdrawal observation
period after the completion of the aforementioned initial treatment. Notably, all the
therapeutic effects observed in the early stage (including improved lactate metabolism,
tissue structure repair, and enhanced indicators related to erectile function) maintained
good sustainability during this period. the relevant data have been included in
Supplementary Figure 11.
We hypothesize that the core reason for this durability of therapeutic effects lies in the
fact that Fbp1-C282S-LNP not only exerts its effects through short-term regulation of
metabolic pathways, but more importantly, it can promote fundamental improvements
in the structural integrity of the corpus cavernosum (such as smooth muscle
regeneration and fibrosis reversal)—functional recovery driven by structural repair
often exhibits a more stable long-term maintenance effect.
At present, we have not yet observed any abnormal effects of this therapeutic strategy
on other metabolic pathways. However, in subsequent studies, we will further deepen
relevant research through metabolomic analysis to more comprehensively evaluate its
metabolic safety.
Once again, we sincerely thank you for your profound inspiration. Your attention has
prompted us to expand our research perspective from "short-term efficacy" to
"long-term benefits", which not only provides more sufficient evidence for the clinical
application potential of this mRNA therapeutic strategy, but also points out a refined
direction for safety assessment in subsequent studies.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This investigation is concerned with the impact of diabetes on erectile dysfunction.
The authors specifically investigate lactate accumulation, the causes of this
accumulation, and its impact on the function of the corpus cavernosum. They propose
that transcriptional and functional repression of Fbp1 is the cause of the lactate
accumulation, and investigate strategies to correct Fbp1 activity and erectile function.
Major concerns – models and approaches
1. The experimental model of diabetes is extreme. A blood glucose concentration
of 30mM is exceptionally high and would be fatal in humans. It is important to
establish whether the findings are consistent in a model system that achieves a
clinically relevant blood glucose concentration.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful comments regarding the clinical
relevance of the diabetic model used in our study. Your feedback is invaluable for
clarifying the rationale behind our model selection and strengthening the translational
value of our findings.
Regarding the blood glucose levels in DMED mouse model, we would like to address
three key points: the rationale for model establishment, its standardization, and its
clinical relevance.
First, the DMED model was established using a well-validated and widely adopted
protocol in the field (PMID: 37217862; PMID: 37445656; PMID: 39536767; PMID:
40041301). The modeling process consisted of two phases: induction of metabolic
disorder via a 4-week high-fat diet, followed by pancreatic β-cell impairment through
five consecutive low-dose streptozotocin injections. Diabetes was confirmed only
when blood glucose levels consistently exceeded 16.7 mmol/L—a threshold aligned
with the clinical definition of hyperglycemia in human diabetes. The elevated glucose
level of 30 mmol/L observed during ED assessment reflects the natural progression of
untreated diabetes, rather than an initial modeling target. This approach is supported
by multiple studies (PMID: 35068334; PMID: 37445656), which have demonstrated
that such glucose levels are well-tolerated in mice and effectively mimic the
pathological state of long-term uncontrolled diabetes, resembling the clinical course
of poorly managed diabetic patients.
Most importantly, the central conclusion of our study does not rely on the absolute
value of hyperglycemia, but rather on the association between lactate accumulation
and DMED. Through clinical sample analysis, we confirmed that blood lactate levels
are significantly elevated in human DMED patients compared to healthy controls and
are positively correlated with ED severity. Although the absolute blood glucose value
in mice is higher than typical clinical readings, the core mechanism of
lactate-mediated ED remains consistent across species. This cross-species mechanistic
alignment underscores the clinical translatability of our findings.
We thank you once again for raising this important point. Your comments have
enabled us to better articulate the scientific basis of model selection, emphasizing that
hyperglycemia is a result of disease progression rather than a model limitation, and
highlighting the critical role of mechanism-backed clinical relevance—significantly
enhancing the credibility and impact of our conclusions.

Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful observation regarding the
difference between the lactate concentrations used in our in vitro experiments (5 mM
and 10 mM) and the plasma lactate levels measured in our animal model (~3 mM).
This question is crucial for evaluating the scientific soundness of our experimental
design, and we are pleased to provide a systematic explanation covering the following
three aspects: clinical and preclinical evidence, rationale for in vitro concentration
gradients, and the scientific basis for the in vitro–in vivo concentration difference.
Firstly, both clinical and animal studies support the presence of elevated lactate levels
in DMED and their correlation with disease severity. With approval from the clinical
ethics committee, we recruited 60 DMED patients and age-matched healthy controls.
Serum lactate was significantly higher in DMED patients, with some exceeding 5
mmol/L, and a clear positive correlation was observed between lactate levels and ED
severity.
In animal models, we confirmed that both serum and corpus cavernosum lactate levels
were markedly increased in DMED mice, and a linear correlation was found between
local and systemic lactate concentrations (Figs. 1F-1H). These results confirm that
high lactate levels do occur in vivo, particularly within diseased tissues, thereby
justifying the use of elevated lactate concentrations in vitro.
Secondly, the lactate concentration gradients used in vitro were carefully designed
based on existing literature and preliminary experiments. In vivo, we tested three
intraperitoneal lactate injection doses (0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 g/kg) referencing
established methods (PMID: 38925041). The 0.5 g/kg dose produced a significant
increase in serum lactate, while 0.75 g/kg did not yield further short-term elevation;
hence, the former was selected for subsequent in vivo studies.
For in vitro experiments, we treated CCSMCs with seven lactate concentrations (0–
12 mmol/L). Pre-experimental data indicated that concentrations ≤4 mmol/L had no
significant effect on cell viability—consistent with reports in the literature (PMID:
38855868; PMID: 36302626)—while concentrations ≥5 mmol/L induced clear
functional alterations. We therefore selected 5 mM and 10 mM as representative low
and high stimulatory concentrations for further study (Figs. 1S–1X).
Lastly, the use of higher lactate concentrations in vitro than those observed
systemically in vivo is scientifically justified and aligns with common practices in
pathological simulation. Isolated cells in vitro are removed from the complex
metabolic and regulatory microenvironment of the body, often requiring higher
stimulus concentrations to elicit responses comparable to those in living tissues.
We thank you once again for raising this important question. Your comments have
allowed us to better articulate the pathological relevance of elevated lactate, the
experimental rationale behind our concentration selection, and the scientific principles
underlying in vitro–in vivo concentration differences—thereby strengthening the
validity and impact of our experimental design. Relevant results supporting the above
points can be found in Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 1.

8. Fig 6B – palmitoylation anchors proteins to membranes. Why does the amount

feedback. Regarding the observation that “Fbp1 palmitoylation decreases upon
ZDHHC13 silencing (Fig. 5), yet its abundance in the cytosolic fraction remains
unchanged,” we would like to offer the following clarification based on our
experimental methodology and the principles of cellular fractionation:
Cytoplasmic and nuclear proteins were separated using a commercial extraction kit
(#P0028, Beyotime), which employs a stepwise lysis protocol. The cytosolic fraction
is obtained under hypotonic conditions that lyse the plasma membrane, releasing
soluble cytoplasmic components. Importantly, this process also generates membrane
fragments—including those from organelles such as mitochondria and the
endoplasmic reticulum—which are inherently present in the cytosolic fraction. As a
result, this fraction contains not only truly soluble proteins but also
membrane-associated proteins (including palmitoylated proteins) that remain attached
to these membrane structures.
In the case of Fbp1, although ZDHHC13 knockdown reduces its palmitoylation level
(which would be expected to weaken membrane association), the cytosolic fraction
still contains both membrane-attached and freely soluble pools of Fbp1. The
combined signal from these two sources may therefore mask a potential change in the
soluble fraction alone. Thus, the unchanged abundance of Fbp1 in the cytosolic
fraction does not contradict the palmitoylation results but rather reflects the
methodological particularity of the fractionation process.

interpretation. Thank you for your valuable contribution to enhancing the quality of

metabolically active cells, thereby reflecting true cell viability rather than merely

concentrations up to and including 4 mmol/L (Sub-Fig. 1K). Thus, 5 mmol/L and 10
mmol/L were selected as low and high lactate stimulation concentrations, respectively,
for subsequent experiments. The CCK-8 assay was used to identify two
concentrations—5 mM and 10 mM lactate—that significantly affected cell viability
(Figure 1T). It is important to emphasize that the experimental objective was
specifically to evaluate the impact of lactate on cell viability, rather than on
proliferative activity alone.

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their insightful comments regarding

appreciate your thoughtful question, which has helped clarify this important
mechanistic detail.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In the present study the authors suggest that excessive lactate accumulation in the
corpus cavernosum is a key pathological driver of DMED, promoting structural
degeneration, smooth muscle cell loss, and erectile dysfunction in diabetic mice.
Mechanistically, they show that transcriptional repression and functional impairment
of Fbp1 (fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1, Fbp1), a rate-limiting gluconeogenic enzyme,
underlined corpus cavernosum lactate pathological accumulation. Epigenetic profiling
revealed that Suv39h1-mediated H3K9 trimethylation and Ezh2-dependent H3K27
trimethylation synergistically suppressed Fbp1 transcription. In addition,
Zdhhc13-mediated palmitoylation at the Fbp1 C282 site further disrupted its
gluconeogenesis related function, aggravating lactate accumulation. To rescue these
defects, the authors engineered Fbp1 C282S-loaded lipid nanoparticles (Fbp1
C282S-LNP), which restored Fbp1 expression and abrogated pathological
palmitoylation in the corpus cavernosum, improving erectile function in DMED mice.
Main points
1-The authors suggested that, compared with the normal mice, the Fbp1
knockout significantly increased the cavernosal lactate and decreased the ICP,
the lumen--to--parenchyma ratio, and the α--Sma fluorescence intensity (Figure
2H -N). Would the administration of LDH inhibitors be beneficial in this
condition (Fbp1 knockout mice with increased Lactate production)?
Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful question regarding whether lactate
dehydrogenase (LDH) inhibitors could confer benefits in Fbp1-/+ mice. This is indeed
a valuable direction for further investigation.
Theoretically, since LDH is a key enzyme catalyzing the conversion of pyruvate to
lactate, LDH inhibitors could potentially reduce lactate production and thereby
alleviate cavernous lactate accumulation resulting from Fbp1 knockout. This
mechanism has been supported in several metabolic disease models (PMID:
38852200; PMID: 38925041). To test this hypothesis, we treated DMED mice with
the LDH inhibitor sodium oxamate (0.5 g/kg, administered intraperitoneally once
daily for two weeks). However, no significant changes in cavernous lactate levels
were observed.
We propose the following explanation: glucose can be rapidly converted to lactate via
glycolysis, while lactate can be reconverted to glucose through gluconeogenesis to
maintain glucose homeostasis (Fig. 2A). Tissue lactate accumulation typically results
from either enhanced glycolysis or impaired gluconeogenesis. Using RNA-seq data
from our established DMED mouse (Fig. 2B) and rat (Fig. 2C) models, we analyzed
the expression of key enzymes in both pathways. The results revealed significant
downregulation of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) at the transcriptional level in
both species. Further analysis of LDH isozymes (Ldha, Ldhb, Ldhc, Ldhd) indicated
widespread transcriptional suppression, suggesting overall inhibition of glycolysis and
reduced lactate production. Therefore, cavernous lactate accumulation in DMED is
more likely attributable to impaired lactate consumption—specifically, deficient
gluconeogenesis—which may explain why LDH inhibition did not significantly alter
lactate levels.
We thank you once again for raising this compelling question, which has deepened
our understanding of the metabolic dysregulation caused by Fbp1 deficiency. The
relevant supplementary figures have been included in the Supplementary Materials.
2- The authors show by ChIP qPCR assay that H3K9me3 or H3K27me3 were
enriched on the promoter of Fbp1 in the MOVAS cells and primary mouse
CCSMCs (Figure 3B, C, Supplementary Figure 1A, B). The promoter should be
better epigenetically characterized by verifying H3K4me3, H3K27ac, DNA
methylation and members of the PRC1 and 2 complexes as well as the active pol
2.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. To address
this point, we further investigated the potential roles of H3K4me3, H3K27ac, active
RNA polymerase II, and the PRC1 complex-associated mark H2AK119ub in the
regulation of FBP1. Using the ChIP-Atlas database, we detected binding signals for
H3K4me3, H3K27ac, RNA polymerase II, and H2AK119ub at the FBP1 promoter
region. These findings were further validated by our ChIP-qPCR experiments.
Additionally, we examined the expression levels of these epigenetic regulators in the
corpus cavernosum tissue of diabetic mice via Western blotting. The results indicated
that the protein levels of most factors remained largely unaltered, with the notable
exception of H3K27ac, which was significantly reduced. We hypothesize that this
decrease may be attributable to competitive occupancy resulting from the
upregulation of H3K27me3, which suppresses H3K27ac enrichment and thereby
impairs its transcriptional activation function.
Regarding the PRC2 complex, we would like to emphasize that EZH2—a core
catalytic subunit of PRC2—was the focus of our previous experiments. We have
clearly demonstrated that EZH2 modulates FBP1 expression through
H3K27me3-mediated repression.
We are truly grateful for the reviewer’s insightful comment, which has greatly
strengthened the mechanistic depth and rigor of our study. All relevant data have been
included in Supplementary Figure 3.
3- In Fig 3 D-E, the authors showed that the enrichment of H3K9me3 or
H3K27me3 were significantly increased in the corpus cavernosum of DMED
mice compared to normal mice (Figure 3D 3E). Is this regulation specific of the
corpus cavernosum? Is it also reported in patients? Is it also at the RNA level?
Many more epi-regulators target H3K9me3 or H3K27me3 in respect of the onec
shown. How is their expression?
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments. Diabetes is
a systemic metabolic disorder, and aberrant epigenetic modifications have been
reported across various tissues under diabetic conditions. For instance, H3K9me3
levels are significantly elevated in diabetic retinopathy (PMID: 34238980) and in
skeletal muscle in the context of diabetes (PMID: 30528377). Similarly, H3K27me3
is markedly upregulated in endothelial cells from diabetic patients (PMID: 38580969).
Moreover, EZH2-mediated H3K27me3 has been demonstrated to play a critical role
in the pathogenesis and progression of diabetes (PMID: 38161208). These findings
suggest that the abnormal increases in H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 are not confined to
the corpus cavernosum but occur across multiple diabetic tissues.
It is important to emphasize that H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 are post-translational
histone modifications and are not regulated at the RNA level. In our preliminary
experiments, we examined the expression of several key histone methyltransferases
associated with these modifications—including SUV39H1, SUV39H2, SETDB1,
SETDB2, EZH1, and EZH2—in the corpus cavernosum of diabetic mice. The results
indicated that among these, the H3K9me3 methyltransferase SUV39H1 and the
H3K27me3 methyltransferase EZH2 showed particularly notable dysregulation.
We thank the reviewer again for their valuable feedback, which has helped us deepen
the mechanistic insight into epigenetic regulation in diabetic conditions.
4- The authors employed PROTAC technology to synthesize a Cbx3 specific
inhibitor by spatially bridging E3 ligase and the target protein, thereby inducing
ubiquitination mediated degradation of Cbx3 (Supplementary Figure 3A, K). In
the methods the authors give a very short description: “PROTAC In designing a
Cbx3 targeting PROTAC, we used a molecular bridging strategy [31]. One
ligand, the H3K9me3 peptide, binds Cbx3 due to its specific recognition ability.
The other, Pomalidomide, attaches to the E3 ubiquitin ligase CRL4CRBN,
widely used in PROTACs for promoting target protein degradation. The bridge
molecule, with optimized length and rigidity, links these two ligands to ensure
effective binding and maintain activity".
From this description, the strategy might also degrade other binders. The
specificity and selectivity of the characterization should be shown in depth.
Please also include dose curves and IC50.
Response:
Response: We sincerely appreciate your careful attention to the experimental evidence
regarding the Cbx3-targeting PROTAC molecule. Your suggestions have provided
essential guidance for systematically clarifying the design rationale, mechanism of
action, and in vivo properties of this compound. Based on experimental data, we
provide the following explanations in logical sequence:
The structural design of the PROTAC molecule, as shown in the schematic diagram,
consists of a Cbx3-binding ligand, a CRBN-recruiting ligand, and an H-shaped linker.
Experimental results confirm that H-PROTAC does not regulate Cbx3 at the
transcriptional level, supporting its action through a post-translational degradation
mechanism. To evaluate the concentration-dependent effect on protein degradation,
CCSMCs were treated with H-PROTAC at six concentrations (0, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, and 5
μM). Cbx3 protein levels were most effectively reduced at 1 μM, which informed the
selection of these concentrations for subsequent experiments.
The specificity of H-PROTAC was validated through multiple experimental
approaches: compared to an A-linker control PROTAC, H-PROTAC exhibited
significantly stronger degradation activity against Cbx3, highlighting the influence of
linker structure on efficacy. Streptavidin pulldown assays further confirmed direct
binding of H-PROTAC to both Cbx3 and CRBN, illustrating its role as a molecular
glue that facilitates target ubiquitination and degradation.
Key pharmacokinetic parameters, including bioavailability and half-life, have been
characterized for H-PROTAC in vivo. Additionally, safety assessments following
intracavernous administration in mice showed no significant abnormalities in liver
and kidney function markers (ALT, AST, BUN, Scr), supporting its preliminary
biosafety and potential for further translational study.
All relevant data have been incorporated into the revised main text and
Supplementary Figure 5 to ensure a comprehensive and logically coherent
presentation. We are grateful for your insightful questions, which have greatly
enhanced the mechanistic clarity and experimental rigor of the PROTAC-related
findings.
5- The authors applied H PROTAC, Chaetocin, and EPZ6438 to the mice with
DMED or Fbp1 knockout. The 3 inhibitors decreased the cavernosal lactate,
partially restored the ICP, the structure and CCSMC content of corpus
cavernosum in DMED mice but had no effect on the Fbp1-knockout mice (Figure
4P, U). Would a combinatory use of the inhibitors display a better therapeutic
value for DMED mice?
Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful question regarding the potential
therapeutic value of combining the three inhibitors—Chaetocin, EPZ6438, and
H-PROTAC. In response, we conducted targeted experiments, and the results are
summarized below:
Although in vitro experiments indicated that simultaneous induction of H3K9me3 and
H3K27me3 led to stronger suppression of Fbp1 expression compared to activating
either pathway alone, suggesting possible molecular synergy, in vivo combination
therapy proved challenging.
Specifically, DMED mice were treated with Chaetocin (intraperitoneal injection),
EPZ6438 (oral gavage), and H-PROTAC (intracavernous injection) using their
respective administration routes. However, after two weeks of combined treatment,
the mice exhibited a significant decline in overall health. Due to these pronounced
adverse effects, which would confound the interpretation of therapeutic outcomes,
the combination regimen was discontinued.
Mechanistically, Fbp1 is regulated through a multi-level network: Suv39h1-mediated
H3K9me3 and EZH2-mediated H3K27me3 synergistically suppress Fbp1
transcription, while ZDHHC13-mediated palmitoylation at C282 impairs Fbp1
enzymatic function, further promoting lactate accumulation. To precisely target these
defects, we developed lipid nanoparticles carrying the Fbp1 C282S mutant (Fbp1
C282S-LNP). This approach not only restores Fbp1 expression in cavernous tissue but
also prevents pathological palmitoylation via the C282S mutation, thereby
concurrently correcting both transcriptional and post-translational deficiencies of
Fbp1 and ultimately improving erectile function in DMED mice.
Although further exploration of optimized drug combinations may be considered,
Fbp1 C282S-LNP currently represents a more targeted and potentially safer
therapeutic strategy, as it specifically addresses the dual dysregulation of Fbp1
without the systemic toxicity associated with multi-drug regimens.
We are grateful for your valuable suggestion, which provides important guidance for
our subsequent research optimization.
6- The authors report CBX3 upregulation in the DMED mice (Fig.3P). Which is
the mechanism(s) behind this deregulation?
Response: This question will be answered together with Question 7.
7- The transcriptome and immunohistochemistry of the corpus cavernosum
showed that the expression of Zdhhc13 was increased in DMED mice (Figure 5K,
L), suggesting that Zdhhc13 may be involved in the palmitoylation of Fbp1 in
vivo. Why is Zdhhc13 overexpressed? Is it tissue specific or?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewers for raising these two critical questions.
You have precisely captured the core mechanistic link between the aberrant
expression of CBX3 and Zdhhc13 in the pathological context of DMED. These
insights are of critical importance for our comprehensive understanding of the
metabolic dysregulation mechanisms in DMED.
Given the limitations of single-target intervention and the toxicity of combined drug
therapy, we next conducted an in-depth investigation into the underlying mechanisms
of Zdhhc13 and Cbx3 upregulation in DMED mice. We performed KEGG pathway
enrichment analysis on differentially expressed genes, which revealed significant
activation of the PI3K-AKT pathway—the most prominently upregulated signaling
pathway in the DMED state.
It is well established that the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway regulates the activity of
SRY-related HMG-box protein 9 (Sox9) [PMID: 33985544, 19711351]. Based on this
research background, we further explored the regulatory association between this
pathway and Zdhhc13/Cbx3. Interestingly, prediction results from the ChIP-Atlas
database showed that Sox9 can bind to the promoter regions of both Zdhhc13 and
Cbx3. Experimental validation confirmed this prediction: we found that the protein
levels of phosphorylated AKT (p-AKT, a marker of PI3K-AKT pathway activation)
and Sox9 were significantly increased in the corpus cavernosum tissue of DMED
mice.
To clarify the regulatory role of Sox9, we conducted functional validation
experiments: in primary mouse CCSMCs, siRNA-mediated knockdown of Sox9
significantly downregulated the expression of Cbx3 and Zdhhc13; conversely,
plasmid-mediated overexpression of Sox9 markedly upregulated their expression.
However, when we delivered adeno-associated virus expressing Sox9-shRNA
(AAV-shSox9) into the corpus cavernosum of DMED mice to inhibit Sox9 activity in
vivo, no significant improvements were observed in cavernosal lactate levels or
intracavernous pressure (ICP).
Taken together, all findings indicate that the Fbp1-C282S-LNP strategy exhibits more
significant advantages: it can directly target the dual defects of Fbp1 (impaired
transcription and pathological palmitoylation), avoiding both the limitations of
single-target intervention and the toxicity risks associated with complex multi-drug
combinations. We sincerely thank the reviewers for their insightful questions, which
have greatly facilitated the refinement of our research mechanisms and therapeutic
strategies. The relevant results have been included in Supplementary Figure 9 and the
revised manuscript.
8- The Fbp1 C282S LNP reduced the cavernosal lactate, improved the ICP and
the structure and CCSMC content, both in DMED and Fbp1 knockout mice
(Figure 7Q, V) supporting that the Fbp1 C282S LNP is a promising therapeutic
strategy for DMED. Were there detected collateral effects for Fbp1 C282S LNP?
Was a Pharmacokinetic and a pharmacodynamic approach be performed?
Response: We greatly appreciate your attention to the characteristics of Fbp1
C282S-LNP across four core dimensions: dose-effect relationship, drug distribution,
pharmacokinetics, and toxicity—these are key indicators for evaluating the safety,
efficacy, and clinical translation potential of the formulation. Based on targeted
experimental designs and data results, we explain each dimension in detail as follows:
To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of Fbp1 C282S-LNPs, we administered
intracavernous injections to DMED mice at three dose levels (0.1 mg/kg, 0.25 mg/kg,
and 0.5 mg/kg), along with a control group. The results indicated that the 0.1 mg/kg
dose did not effectively reduce lactate levels in the corpus cavernosum or improve
erectile function. In contrast, the 0.25 mg/kg dose significantly decreased lactate
accumulation and enhanced erectile performance. The 0.5 mg/kg dose did not yield
statistically superior efficacy compared to the 0.25 mg/kg group, suggesting that 0.25
mg/kg is an effective dose approaching pharmacodynamic saturation.
Multiplex immunofluorescence staining (using Flag tag for Fbp1 C282S-LNPs, and
markers for endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and fibroblasts: vWF, α-SMA, and
vimentin, respectively) revealed strong LNP uptake in smooth muscle cells, with
detectable internalization in endothelial cells and fibroblasts. This indicates that the
LNPs can target multiple relevant cell types within the penile tissue.
Further pharmacokinetic analysis via LC-MS/MS of orbital blood samples showed
that Fbp1 C282S-LNPs have an elimination half-life of 12.57±1.51 hours. To assess
tissue distribution and potential off-target effects, DiD-labeled LNPs were used: the
highest fluorescence intensity was observed in the corpus cavernosum at 0.25 hours
post-injection, followed by a gradual decline, confirming rapid target tissue
accumulation and sustained local concentration. In the liver—the primary clearance
organ—fluorescence intensity initially increased and then decreased without abnormal
retention. Only minimal fluorescence was detected in skeletal muscle and the spleen,
and due to the blood-brain barrier, brain fluorescence remained negligible throughout,
effectively ruling out central nervous system exposure. Additionally, measurements of
liver and kidney function markers (ALT, AST, serum creatinine, and blood urea
nitrogen) showed no significant differences between treated and control groups,
supporting the absence of hepatorenal toxicity.
It is worth emphasizing that although LNPs were taken up by both penile and
non-penile tissues (such as liver and skeletal muscle), we believe this “non-strict
targeting” profile enhances rather than diminishes therapeutic efficacy through two
complementary mechanisms: uptake in liver and muscle enhances systemic lactate
metabolism, thereby reducing lactate delivery to the corpus cavernosum; meanwhile,
uptake within penile endothelial cells and fibroblasts contributes to local lactate
consumption. Thus, the broad targeting capability of LNPs supports a synergistic
therapeutic strategy combining local and systemic effects, with no significant adverse
effects observed.
All relevant data—including dose-response outcomes, pharmacokinetic parameters,
tissue distribution, cellular uptake, and safety assessments—have been added as
Figure 7 and Supplementary Figure 10 in the revised manuscript. These results
collectively support the therapeutic potential and safety of Fbp1 C282S-LNPs. We are
truly grateful for your thorough and insightful comments, which have helped us
present these findings more comprehensively and strengthen the overall rigor of our
study.
9- The methods section should be deeply revised, implementing all details. If
there is space limitation, likely it might go into the additional materials.
Response: We greatly appreciate your feedback. We fully recognize the critical
importance of providing comprehensive methodological details. We sincerely
apologize for our previous omission of sufficient experimental descriptions due to
concerns regarding manuscript length.
In the revised manuscript, we have now expanded the “Methods” section in full,
including detailed specifications of all experimental procedures—such as reagent
models, instrument parameters, and key steps in operational protocols. For certain
specialized protocols and reagent preparation procedures that exceed the space
limitations of the main text, we have provided extended descriptions in the
