Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
The study is interesting and consistent with recent data showing high lactate level in
patients with diabetes. The authors have performed an extensive series of studies to
demonstrate that fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (Fbp1) was reduced in a model of
diabetes induced by high fat diet and STZ. The reduction of Fbp1 was associated with
palmitoylation via Zdhhc13. Restoration of Fbp1 via a lipid nanovesicle injection
directly into the corpus cavernosum restored erectile dysfunction.
Major comments
1. Additional models of diabetes such as db/db mice and type 1 models should be
evaluated as well as patient samples
Response:
We sincerely appreciate your valuable comments, which have provided significant
support for our research. The specific supplementary research contents are as follows:
First, we obtained approval from the Clinical Ethics Committee ( LYEC2025-0188).
We then enrolled 60 DMED patients (including 33 mild, 19 moderate, and 8 severe
cases) along with 60 age-matched healthy controls. Systematic measurement of serum
lactate levels revealed significantly higher lactate in DMED patients (2.4 mmol/L)
compared to healthy controls (1.7 mmol/L; p= 0.0002). This elevation aligns with the
increased lactate levels observed in both serum and corpus cavernosum tissue in our
DMED mouse model, providing clinical evidence supporting the role of lactate in the
pathophysiology of DMED.
It should be noted that, due to ethical and practical constraints, we were unable to
directly measure local lactate concentrations in the corpus cavernosum of DMED
patients. However, in our DMED mouse model, we confirmed a significant positive
correlation between plasma and corpus cavernosum lactate levels. This supports the
inference that local lactate concentrations may also be elevated in human DMED
patients, strengthening the translational relevance of our animal data.
To further evaluate the clinical association between lactate and DMED, we divided all
120 participants into three tertiles based on serum lactate levels: lower (<1/3), middle
(1/3–2/3), and upper (>2/3). The results showed: In the overall cohort, the incidence
of erectile dysfunction (ED) increased significantly across lactate tertiles (p= 0.002),
with the upper tertile showing a significantly higher incidence than the lower tertile
(p= 0.001; Cramer’s V = 0.376). Post-hoc pairwise comparisons were performed
using the chi-square partition method with a corrected significance level of α' = 0.017.
Among DMED patients, the incidence of moderate-to-severe ED also rose with
increasing lactate levels (p= 0.014). The incidence of severe ED was significantly
higher in the upper lactate tertile than in the lower tertile (p= 0.004; Cramer’s V =
0.376). These results not only confirm the association between elevated lactate and
DMED but also reveal a dose-response relationship, thereby enhancing the clinical
applicability of our conclusions.
A type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) mouse model was established using a published
protocol [PMID: 40196453]: 8-week-old male C57BL/6 mice were fasted for 12
hours and injected intraperitoneally with streptozotocin (STZ; 150 mg/kg). Diabetes
was confirmed if fasting blood glucose exceeded 16.7 mmol/L at 72 hours
post-injection. Mice were maintained for 8 weeks before erectile function was
assessed via apomorphine test. Additionally, 20-week-old male db/db mice
(C57BLKS/J-leprdb/leprdb) were obtained from Shulaibao Biotechnology Co., Ltd.
(Wuhan, China).
Fbp1 C282S-loaded lipid nanoparticles (Fbp1 C282S-LNP) were evaluated in both
T1DM and db/db models. The formulation demonstrated significant therapeutic
effects in both models: it effectively reduced cavernous lactate levels, improved
fibrosis, increased smooth muscle content, and enhanced intracavernous pressure .
The efficacy trends were consistent with those observed in the DMED mouse model.
We sincerely thank you for your insightful suggestions. These supplementary studies
strengthen both the clinical and preclinical evidence linking lactate to DMED and
underscore the therapeutic potential of Fbp1 C282S-LNP across multiple models,
significantly enhancing the comprehensiveness and reliability of our research.
2. No discussion of endothelial dysfunction was described which has been
previously found to play a key role in human erectile dysfunction.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your valuable feedback. We fully agree that
endothelial dysfunction is a well-established key mechanism underlying DMED. As
extensively documented, endothelial cells regulate blood flow within the penile
corpus cavernosum through the release of vasoactive substances such as nitric oxide
(NO), and their impairment directly compromises the vasodilatory response essential
for erection [PMID: 26878803].
In recent years, alongside the classical focus on endothelial dysfunction, smooth
muscle cell dysfunction has gradually emerged as another critical research focus in
erectile dysfunction, with several important advances reported [PMID: 37353497;
38874549]. The primary objective of this study is to elucidate how diabetes-induced
lactate accumulation impairs erectile function. Therefore, our in vitro experiments
specifically center on the damaging effects of lactate on smooth muscle cells and the
underlying mechanisms—though this focus does not diminish the central role of
endothelial cells in DMED pathogenesis.
Notably, in our experimental system, Fbp1 C282S-LNP is taken up not only by
smooth muscle cells but also by endothelial cells and other cell types. This
multi-cellular uptake likely contributes synergistically to reducing lactate levels in the
cavernous tissue of DMED mice. The resulting improvement in the metabolic
microenvironment should help support the functional integrity of various penile cell
types—including the vasodilatory capacity of endothelial cells—thereby collectively
contributing to the restoration of normal erectile function.
We acknowledge a limitation of our current study: we did not systematically analyze
specific functional changes in endothelial cells following lactate reduction, nor did we
fully elucidate the synergistic interactions between endothelial and smooth muscle
cells during functional recovery. Accordingly, we have further supplemented the
discussion on endothelial cells in the Discussion section. Future studies will focus on
clarifying how “metabolic repair” coordinately improves DMED across smooth
muscle cells, endothelial cells, and other relevant cell types, thereby providing a more
comprehensive understanding of the pathophysiology of this condition.
We are truly grateful for your insightful comments, which have helped us better
recognize the limitations of our current work and will significantly contribute to
improving the depth and completeness of our research.
3. The results suggest that Zdhhc13 mediated S-palmitoylation on Fbp1
decreases its gluconeogenesis function, but the therapeutic potential of Zdhhc13
inhibition in DMED mice remains limited. It is possible that Fbp1 C282S-loaded
lipid nanoparticles (Fbp1 C282S-LNP) can restore Fbp1 expression and
abrogated pathological palmitoylation in the corpus cavernosum and restore
erectile dysfunction. However priapism should be avoided and different models
should be tested.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful comment. We have evaluated the
therapeutic potential of Fbp1 C282S-loaded lipid nanoparticles (Fbp1 C282S-LNP) in
multiple diabetic models, including type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) mice, type 2
diabetes mellitus (T2DM) models, and db/db mice. In these studies, Fbp1 C282S-LNP
consistently restored Fbp1 expression in the corpus cavernosum, eliminated
pathological palmitoylation, and improved erectile function. Importantly, no priapism
(persistent abnormal erection) was observed during treatment in any of these models,
nor in the pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, or safety studies conducted in normal
mice.
We are grateful for your suggestion, which prompted us to further validate both the
safety and efficacy of Fbp1 C282S-LNP across different models, thereby significantly
enhancing the reliability of our conclusions.
Summary
In summary, we have fully addressed all reviewers’ comments. The revised
manuscript now includes the following key improvements:
1. Added clinical data linking lactate accumulation to erectile dysfunction in DMED
patients, clarified the physiological relevance of lactate levels, and strengthened the
clinical relevance of the study.
2. Provided mechanistic validations: transcriptomic analysis of lactate-induced
smooth muscle cell injury, demonstration of ZDHHC13-downregulation-mediated
FBP1 conformational change (exposure of G260 impairing gluconeogenesis), and
investigation into the upregulation mechanisms of ZDHHC13/CBX3.
3. Supplemented with Fbp1-C282S-LNPs data (dose response, pharmacokinetics,
tissue distribution, hepatorenal toxicity) and extended validation to additional diabetic
mouse models (T1DM, db/db), enhancing translational value.
4. Ensured full methodological transparencyand improved figure clarity and
presentation.
5. Standardized language, terminology, and figure formatting throughout.
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their insightful comments, which have greatly
improved the quality of our manuscript.
Response to Reviewers
We sincerely thank the Editors and Reviewers once again for their valuable time,
meticulous re-evaluation, and insightful supplementary feedback. We have carefully
considered every additional comment and have revised the manuscript accordingly.
We believe these revisions have further strengthened the rigor, completeness, and
clarity of our work. Below, we provide a detailed point-by-point response to each
comment. All changes and supplementary content in the revised manuscript are
highlighted for easy reference.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have substantially and thoughtfully addressed nearly all 15 of the raised
concerns. Their rebuttal includes new experimental data (e.g., longitudinal lactate
measurements, collagen immunofluorescence, PK/PD profiles), mechanistic
clarifications (Zdhhc13-mediated palmitoylation, Cbx3 transcriptional repression),
and translational considerations (clinical serum lactate data, safety/tissue distribution
of LNPs).
While the responses are comprehensive, a few areas could still be strengthened,
including:
1. More detailed quantitative analyses (effect sizes, fibrosis morphometry,
longitudinal statistics).
Response: We sincerely appreciate your positive recognition of our comprehensive
revisions and constructive feedback on further strengthening the manuscript’s
quantitative rigor. We fully agree that detailed quantitative analyses are essential to
reinforcing the reliability and biological relevance of our findings.
As requested, we have supplemented detailed longitudinal statistical analyses for
cavernosal lactate and intracavernous pressure. The results confirm a statistically
significant increase over time in the DMED group. These new analyses are presented
in Supplementary Figures 1d-1f, and described in the main text.
In direct response to your suggestion, we have now calculated and reported effect
sizes for key quantitative comparisons. For comparisons between two groups using
the unpaired t-test, we calculated Cohen's d value, as it is the most appropriate and
widely accepted measure of standardized effect size for this statistical test. It provides
a clear interpretation of the magnitude of the difference between groups, independent
of sample size. For one-way ANOVA analyses involving multiple groups, we first
calculated the overall effect size using eta-squared (η²) and reported the Cohen's d
value for the relevant pairwise post-hoc comparisons. The values are now reported in
the respective figure legends. Additionally, we have supplemented sample sizes (n
values) and detailed statistical methods in the panel of each figure legend, ensuring
full transparency for reproducibility.
We sincerely thank you for your valuable suggestion regarding the need for detailed
fibrosis morphometric analysis. In response, we conducted a systematic and in-depth
re-analysis of our existing histology and immunofluorescence images. Upon careful
examination, we found that our results are consistent with the majority of existing
reports in this research field [PMID: 36064453;32693824；38874549；39536767；
37157936]. In the DMED model, the core characteristic of fibrotic deposition is a
significant quantitative increase in collagen content, whereas under the resolution of
our current methodologies (conventional histological staining), no consistent or
significant differences in the higher-order architecture (i.e., morphology) were
detected. We fully understand and agree with your insightful perspective that more
subtle morphological differences may require more advanced techniques for detection.
The absence of observed significant morphological changes in this study may indeed
reflect the detection limits of the conventional methods we employed.
We sincerely thank you for your insightful guidance, which has helped us refine the
quantitative presentation of our findings, standardize statistical reporting, and clarify
the nature of fibrosis-related changes in our model—further enhancing the rigor and
comprehensiveness of our work.
2. Additional causal validation (e.g., autophagy inhibition rescue, metabolic flux
tracing).
Response: We sincerely appreciate the valuable suggestion regarding the necessity of
supplementing causal validation experiments. We fully concur that in-depth
mechanistic verification is pivotal for establishing the pathophysiological association
between lactate and DMED.
In the previous revision round, transcriptome sequencing revealed that lactate
treatment activates the autophagic pathway in CCSMCs. In response to your
recommendation, we have performed more rigorous causal validation in the current
revision.
In vitro experiments were conducted by pretreating CCSMCs with the autophagy
inhibitor 3-methyladenine (3-MA). The results demonstrated that 3-MA significantly
abrogates lactate-induced excessive autophagy activation, impairment of cell viability,
and phenotypic switching toward the synthetic smooth muscle phenotype.
In animal models, we further analyzed autophagic activity in the corpus cavernosum
of lactate-challenged mice and DMED mice. Intriguingly, progressive elevation of the
LC3-II/LC3-I ratio was observed in both models during disease progression, whereas
P62 protein expression exhibited a dynamic change characterized by an initial
decrease followed by a subsequent increase. This finding suggests that autophagic
flux may become dysregulated in the late stage of the disease.
Building upon these observations, we performed interventions with 3-MA and
SMER28, respectively. Our data showed that 3-MA effectively suppressed excessive
autophagy and remarkably improved erectile function as well as tissue architecture in
DMED mice. In contrast, although SMER28 promoted P62 degradation, it failed to
exert significant therapeutic efficacy.
Finally, we validated that Fbp1 C282S-LNP treatment can also efficiently reverse
autophagic abnormalities in the corpus cavernosum of DMED mice.
Collectively, these results indicate that lactate-induced excessive autophagy is a key
mechanism contributing to corpus cavernosum smooth muscle cell damage.
Furthermore, CCSMCs were cultured with 2 mM ¹³C-labeled lactate under starvation
conditions, and the extracellular medium was analyzed by nuclear magnetic resonance
(NMR) spectroscopy referring to relevant literature [PMID：12944325, PMID：
10751328, PMID：10600777]. We successfully detected the production of ¹³C-labeled
glucose, which directly confirms that CCSMCs possess gluconeogenic capacity to
convert lactate into glucose. This finding provides direct experimental evidence
supporting the central role of lactate metabolism in CCSMCs.
3. Longer-term follow-up and repeat-dose safety data to enhance translational
relevance.
Response:We are grateful for this insightful comment regarding the long-term safety
profile and therapeutic sustainability of the Fbp1 C282S-LNP strategy, which
represent key considerations for its clinical translation. In our previous revision, a
preliminary assessment of treatment durability was conducted, incorporating a
one-month treatment-free observation period following the initial 4-week therapy. It is
noteworthy that the principal therapeutic benefits—including improved lactate
metabolism, tissue repair, and erectile function—were consistently maintained
throughout this follow-up interval (Supplementary Figure 16). These observations
suggest that the intervention may promote sustained and restorative outcomes beyond
transient symptomatic amelioration.
We fully concur that a more systematic evaluation of long-term safety and repeated
dosing regimens is essential to further de-risk this therapeutic strategy. A study
designed to comprehensively address these aspects would require an extended
timeline with multiple treatment cycles and detailed systemic toxicity monitoring,
which lies beyond the scope of the present discovery-phase investigation.
In response to your suggestion, we have added a dedicated paragraph in the
Discussion section to acknowledge this direction and outline future work: "Although
sustained treatment effects were observed following short-term intervention in
this study, further investigation is warranted to elucidate the long-term safety
profile and optimal dosing frequency of Fbp1 C282S-LNP. Subsequent studies
employing extended multi-dose regimens in larger animal models will be
valuable to comprehensively assess chronic toxicity and maximize the
translational potential of this strategy."
We thank you again for this suggestion, which has enhanced the clinical relevance and
scholarly rigor of our work.
4. Schematic figures in the introduction or discussion to better communicate the
proposed mechanism.
Overall, the revisions substantially improve the manuscript, and the study now
provides a clearer mechanistic insight and stronger therapeutic rationale for targeting
Fbp1/lactate metabolism in DMED. I believe the paper is much closer to being
suitable for publication after minor additional clarifications.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the suggestion to add a schematic diagram in the
main text for a clearer presentation of the mechanism pathway. In response to your
recommendation, we have inserted a fully annotated mechanism schematic (Figure 8)
along with relevant textual explanations in the Discussion section of the paper:
Transcriptional repression and functional dysfunction of Fbp1 are key causes of
penile cavernosal lactate accumulation in DMED. Mechanistically, H3K9me3
mediated by the Suv39h1/Cbx3 complex and H3K27me3 mediated by Ezh2
cooperatively suppress Fbp1 transcription; meanwhile, Zdhhc13-mediated
palmitoylation of the FBP1 protein at the C282 site directly impairs its
gluconeogenic function, exacerbating lactate accumulation. To target the
aforementioned aberrant mechanisms, we developed Fbp1 C282S-LNP, which
restores Fbp1 expression and blocks pathological palmitoylation via
intracavernosal injection, thereby effectively reducing local lactate levels.
We believe that the inclusion of this schematic diagram significantly enhances the
visual presentation of the mechanism pathway in the paper, enabling readers to more
intuitively comprehend the logical connection between the molecular mechanisms and
the therapeutic strategy. We sincerely thank you again for this valuable suggestion,
which has played a crucial role in improving the quality of the paper.
Reviewer #6 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Xiao et al identifies fructose 1,6 bisphosphatase 1 (FBP1) activity
in corpus cavernosum smooth muscle cells (CCSMCs) as a potentially important
component to erectile function in mice and the overall health of CCSMCs. This is by
virtue of FBP1's role in the gluconeogenic pathway, which the authors claim is
necessary to prevent lactate accumulation that may otherwise impair CCSMC
function. The implications are significant because this study provides a potentially
novel target for ED treatment that could in theory be used alone or in conjunction
with traditional therapies such as phosphodiesterase inhibitors.
The authors report that FBP1 expression and function in CCSMCs is reduced in a
model of diabetes mellitus-induced erectile dysfuncton(DMED). This happens as a
result of epigenetic and post-translational events, leading ultimately to elevated lactate
concentrations in the corpus cavernosum. The authors go to great lengths to identify
the mechanistic basis for changes in FBP1 expression (via histone methylation
pathways) and functon(via palmitoylation), using in vitro methods as well as their
mouse model of DMED. The molecular biology experiments are fairly thorough by
design (although underpowered), and complimentary approaches are used. In
particular, the use of lipid nanoparticles to deliver palmitoylation-resistant FBP1 is a
compelling approach to correct aberrant metabolic processes.
While concerns raised by Reviewer 2 on palmitoylation were adequately addressed by
authors, there are several major issues, described below, which diminish the overall
impact of the manuscript. In general, while many of the experiments shed light on the
regulatory mechanisms controlling the functional expression of FBP1 in various
systems, extrapolation of these findings to the author's central hypothesis is limited by
several concerns.
Major concerns:
1 - The central hypothesis of the manuscript rests on the idea that dysregulation
of FBP1 in CCSMCs leads to lactate accumulation via suppression of
gluconeogenesis. However, the authors do not provide evidence, nor do they cite
previous work showing that CCSMCs actually carry out gluconeogenesis to a
significant degree. Aside from transcript-level data and a western blot showing
that a few other gluconeogenic enzymes were not altered the corpus cavernosum
of DMED mice (Sup Fig 2), there is no supporting evidence that lactate
accumulation in the corpus cavernosum happens as a result impaired flux
through the gluconeogenic pathway within CCSMCs. Relying on the
quantification of enzyme abundance, rather than measuring glucose or
metabolite production directly, is not a rigorous way to test the extent to which
glycolytic or gluconeogenic pathways proceed in CCSMCs under the
experimental conditions. Without a clear demonstration that CCSMCs carry out
gluconeogenesis and that inhibition of this pathway specifically leads to lactate
accumulation, it is impossible to interpret the study's findings in the context of
the authors' proposed model. The authors must definitively show that
CCSMC-localized FB1 participates in "lactate clearance via gluconeogenesis," so
to speak, otherwise the premise of the study is not sound.
The authors do mention that conversion of lactate into glucose via the Cori Cycle
is a key part of lactate metabolism. However, in this pathway, lactate generated
by muscle under anaerobic conditions is converted to glucose in the liver. If a
similar pathway exists within smooth muscle cells, the authors should include a
reference which describes it. Likewise, many of the references to FBP1 function
in lactate metabolism and/or diabetic models involve studies using liver cells or
liver tissue. It is not appropriate to draw parallels between the findings of this
study and others that deal with these pathways specifically in the liver.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your insightful comments. You correctly noted
that establishing the functional gluconeogenic capacity of corpus cavernosum smooth
muscle cells (CCSMCs) is a core premise of this study. To address this, we have
reviewed foundational work in the field and integrated our experimental data to
provide the following systematic evidence:
Smooth muscle cells have been shown to possess complete gluconeogenic capacity
and independent gluconeogenic metabolic compartments [PMID: 8789645]. Fbp1, a
key functional enzyme in this pathway, catalyzes the critical conversion of exogenous
fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to glucose [PMID: 10600777] and exhibits unique
subcellular localization in smooth muscle cells [PMID: 16200456]. Pathological
studies further underscore Fbp1’s functional importance—for instance,
downregulation of gluconeogenic enzymes (including Fbp1) during vascular
calcification correlates closely with metabolic imbalance [PMID: 21757657].
Collectively, these findings confirm Fbp1 as a functional, indispensable key enzyme
for gluconeogenesis in smooth muscle cells. Unlike hepatic gluconeogenesis (which
maintains systemic glucose homeostasis), CCSMC gluconeogenesis may support
local energy demands (e.g., during erection) or clear lactate (preventing local
acidosis-induced impairment of smooth muscle contraction).
Second, building on this theoretical framework, we provide direct experimental
evidence via metabolic flux analysis. Primary mouse CCSMCs were cultured with 2
mM ¹³C-labeled lactate under starvation conditions; nuclear magnetic resonance
(NMR) detected ¹³C-labeled glucose production, directly confirming CCSMCs’
gluconeogenic capacity.
More importantly, we established a complete causal evidence chain in animal models:
(1) DMED models showed reduced Fbp1 expression and lactate accumulation in
cavernous tissue; (2) Fbp1+/- mice exhibited significantly elevated cavernous lactate
levels; (3) Fbp1 C282S-LNP was extensively taken up by CCSMCs, restoring
functional Fbp1 expression in cavernous tissue, reducing lactate levels, and improving
erectile function.
Additionally, analyses of oxygen consumption rate (OCR), extracellular acidification
rate (ECAR), and glucose/lactate production flux in the MOVAS cell line further
support Fbp1’s critical role in regulating smooth muscle cell metabolic homeostasis.
However, we acknowledge that limitations in primary cell acquisition prevented
replication of some energy metabolism experiments in primary cells—an inherent
constraint of primary cell research.
In summary, through systematic literature review, direct metabolic flux validation,
and in vitro/in vivo functional experiments, we provide multi-level evidence for our
core hypothesis: "Impaired FBP1 function in CCSMCs causes lactate accumulation
by inhibiting gluconeogenesis." Thank you for your valuable input, which has
strengthened the rigor of our argument.
2 - Throughout the study, elevations in lactate concentration, either systemically
or locally, are reported in association with functional/structural/biochemical
changes in the corpus cavernosum. However, these observations are correlative
and there is a lack of evidence suggesting the downstream effects are a direct
result of lactate accumulation consequent to suppressed gluconeogenesis/FBP1
activity within CCSMCs. In addition, there should be more discussion of how
excessive lactate might cause the phenotypic effects that are described. What is
the underlying pathological mechanism by which lactate accumulation causes
dysfunction?
Response: We sincerely appreciate this important comment of yours. You correctly
pointed out the need to clarify the causal relationship between lactate accumulation
and the observed functional dysfunction, as well as to further elaborate on its
underlying pathological mechanism. We have addressed this issue through
supplementary experiments and in-depth discussions.
To confirm that the observed phenotypic changes are a direct consequence of lactate
accumulation, we conducted gain-of-function and rescue experiments both in vitro
and in vivo:In in vitro experiments, we treated CCSMCs with exogenous sodium
lactate (5 mM and 10 mM). The results showed that key pathological
changes—including decreased cell viability and phenotypic switching—exhibited a
dose-dependent pattern, demonstrating lactate’s direct damaging effect. In animal
experiments, intraperitoneal injection of sodium lactate into healthy mice successfully
increased lactate levels in the corpus cavernosum, accompanied by significant
impairment of erectile function and histological changes that recapitulated the core
pathological features of DMED. Most compellingly, targeted restoration of Fbp1
function in the corpus cavernosum using Fbp1 C282S-LNPs effectively reduced
lactate accumulation and reversed both erectile dysfunction and tissue damage in
DMED mice. This rescue experiment confirms that correcting lactate metabolic
dysregulation is sufficient to improve the disease phenotype.
We fully understand and highly agree with your insightful suggestion regarding the
need to further strengthen the evidence chain for lactate’s downstream mechanism of
action—this profound perspective helps establish a causal link confirming that lactate
accumulation is a direct cause of cavernous dysfunction.
In the previous revision, transcriptome sequencing revealed that lactate treatment
activates the autophagic pathway in CCSMCs.
Following your recommendation, we performed more rigorous mechanistic validation
in the current revision:
In vitro experiments demonstrated that the autophagy inhibitor 3-methyladenine
(3-MA) significantly suppressed lactate-induced excessive autophagy, impaired cell
viability, and phenotypic switching.
Animal experiments further showed that in both lactate-challenged mice and DMED
mice, the ratio of the autophagy marker LC3-II/LC3-I was elevated, while P62 protein
expression exhibited dynamic changes—suggesting dysregulated autophagic flux.
Intervention experiments revealed that the autophagy inhibitor 3-MA effectively
improved erectile function and tissue structure in DMED mice, whereas the
autophagy enhancer SMER28, despite promoting P62 degradation, exerted no
significant therapeutic effect.
Finally, we validated that Fbp1 C282S-LNP treatment can also efficiently reverse
autophagic abnormalities in the corpus cavernosum of DMED mice.
These results indicate that lactate-induced excessive autophagy is a key mechanism
underlying corpus cavernosum smooth muscle cell damage.
We believe that these newly supplemented experimental data, together with our
existing evidence, form a complete causal evidence chain, clearly defining the
pathological mechanism: "lactate accumulation → excessive autophagy → cell
damage → functional dysfunction." We again thank you for your valuable comments,
which have played a pivotal role in enhancing the mechanistic depth of our study.
3 - Do the authors suggest that lactate is produced in CCSMCs under aerobic
conditions? Does oxygen availability in corpus cavernosum have an impact on
lactate generation? Is it possible that aerobic metabolism is somehow impaired in
CCSMCs in the DMED model, and that this leads to lactate accumulation
independently of FBP1? If there are other metabolic disturbances in CCSMCs in
the DMED model, the mechanism(s) leading to lactate accumulation may or may
not be connected to the functional impairment of the corpus cavernosum. As
mentioned above, it would be helpful to discuss a clear mechanistic link between
excessive lactate and impaired CCSMC function.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the series of profound questions you raised, which have been
crucial for refining the demonstration of metabolic mechanisms in this study.
First, regarding lactate production under aerobic conditions, previous studies have
indeed shown that even under aerobic conditions, normal metabolic activity generates
small amounts of lactate due to the metabolic compartmentalization of glycolysis and
gluconeogenesis in cells—though lactate production increases significantly under
hypoxic conditions. We also fully acknowledge that oxygen supply to the corpus
cavernosum is a important factor influencing lactate levels, and several studies have
confirmed that the pathological process of DMED is closely associated with local
hypoxia.
Your question regarding "whether other metabolic disorders contribute to lactate
accumulation in the DMED model" is highly insightful. We honestly acknowledge
that this study focuses on elucidating the mechanism of reduced lactate clearance
mediated by FBP1 dysfunction. Our data—such as the downregulated transcriptional
levels of key glycolytic enzymes—indicate that in the DMED model used in this
study, lactate accumulation is more likely driven by impaired clearance. Additionally,
we attempted to inhibit glycolysis using an LDHA inhibitor, but this did not
significantly reduce cavernous lactate levels. Of course, we cannot completely rule
out the possibility of other pathways (e.g., impaired aerobic metabolism), and these
complex metabolic interactions undoubtedly represent important directions for future
research.
Nevertheless, our series of functional experiments strongly confirm that the
FBP1-mediated lactate metabolic pathway plays an indispensable core role in DMED:
manipulating FBP1 function directly affects lactate levels, and restoring FBP1
function via Fbp1 C282S-LNPs specifically improves local lactate metabolism and
rescues erectile function. This demonstrates that this pathway is a sufficient and
important cause of functional dysfunction.
Finally, we fully agree with your insight that a clear mechanistic link between
excessive lactate and impaired CCSMC function must be established. This was one of
the core focuses of our current revision. As addressed in the previous response,
following your suggestion, we confirmed through experiments that lactate-induced
excessive autophagy is the key link in the causal chain connecting these two processes,
and we have included an in-depth discussion of this mechanism.
We again thank you for your insightful questions, which have greatly enhanced the
logical rigor and mechanistic depth of our study.
4 - In the model of the heterozygous Fbp1-/+ mice, genetic disruption is global,
making it difficult to parse out local effects in the corpus cavernosum from
effects elsewhere in the body (i.e., the liver). Is it possible that metabolic
disruption from global Fbp1-/+ produces the functional changes in CCSMCs as
part of a broader systemic phenotype? Is it possible that CCSMC dysfunction
happens coincidentally with an elevation in circulating lactate, but not
necessarily because of it? This does not rule out the possibility that elevated
circulating lactate in Fbp1-/+ mice has a detrimental effect on CCSMCs, but it is
difficult to justify the conclusion that CCSMC-localized FBP1 dysregulation is
driving the observed effects.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate this profound, critical question. Your insight into the
limitations of the Fbp1+/- heterozygous mouse model—and concern about potential
confounding between systemic metabolic disorders and local effects—are entirely
reasonable and well-founded. This has prompted us to interpret our conclusions more
cautiously and strengthen support for the local mechanism with supplementary
experiments.
You correctly noted that in the systemic Fbp1+/- model, distinguishing between
cavernous local effects and systemic impacts (e.g., hyperlactatemia from impaired
hepatic gluconeogenesis) is challenging. Systemically elevated lactate could
independently exert direct toxic effects on corpus cavernosum smooth muscle cells
(CCSMCs), causing dysfunction. We fully agree that phenotypic data from Fbp1+/-
mice alone would be insufficient to conclude "local FBP1 dysfunction in CCSMCs
drives the phenotype."
It is noteworthy that we observed elevated plasma lactate levels in clinical patients
with DMED, and lactate concentration was significantly correlated with both the
occurrence and severity of the condition. In a DMED mouse model, we similarly
found increased lactate levels in both plasma and penile tissues. Through in vivo and
in vitro experiments, we further validated the dose-dependent detrimental effect of
lactate on CCSMCs and erectile function. More importantly, after administration of
Fbp1-C282S-LNP, tissue distribution analysis revealed that the nanoparticles
preferentially accumulated in the corpus cavernosum, where they were efficiently
taken up by CCSMCs. This led to a significant reduction in intracavernosal lactate
levels and a marked improvement in the erectile function phenotype of DMED mice.
In the current round of experiments, we further added immunofluorescence
staining and quantitative tissue analysis of the liver, skeletal muscle, and penile
corpus cavernosum. Crucially, pharmacokinetic data first showed Fbp1 C282S-LNPs
(administered via local cavernous injection) were primarily retained in the injected
penis. While minor accumulation was detected in the liver and skeletal muscle over
time, the combined results of immunofluorescence staining and quantitative tissue
analysis confirmed that only the penile corpus cavernosum exhibited a statistically
significant increase in Fbp1 protein expression—no significant changes were
observed in the liver or skeletal muscle.
These results strongly suggest that elevated lactate levels localized in the corpus
cavernosum impair CCSMC function and erectile function, and that the corresponding
therapeutic effect is primarily driven by the specific upregulation of FBP1 within the
cavernous tissue, rather than indirect systemic metabolic modulation. We fully agree
with your emphasis on methodological rigor, which has helped us sharpen the focus
and strengthen the core argument of our study. Relevant clarifications have been
incorporated into the revised manuscript, and we thank you again for your insightful
feedback.
5 - Apomorphine, the drug used to induce erection in mice, is a centrally acting
dopamine receptor agonist targeting dopamine signaling pathways in the brain.
It is thought to be most effective for psychogenic erectile dysfuncton(in humans)
and works via a mechanism separate from PDE inhibitors, which act locally.
How do the authors rule out that experimental interventions (DMED model,
lactate injection, metabolic changes from Fbp1-/+, etc.) do not interfere with
neural control of erectile function?
Response: We sincerely appreciate the important question you raised. You correctly
pointed out that apomorphine, as a central dopamine receptor agonist, induces
erections primarily by activating dopamine signaling pathways in the central nervous
system—this mechanism differs from the local action of PDE5 inhibitors. We fully
agree that excluding potential interference of experimental interventions on the neural
control pathway of erections is crucial for ensuring the reliability of our study’s
conclusions.
We can clearly rule out such interference through the following experimental design
and results:
First, in the different animal models involved in this study, the use of apomorphine
was strictly limited to baseline screening of erectile function in DMED model mice
(i.e., administered only once after model establishment and before grouping for
intervention). This step was used to verify whether the animals had successfully
developed an ED model and possessed inducible erectile potential, which is a
commonly used method in DMED model establishment [PMID: 41090037; 40676888;
39654344]. In contrast, in the Fbp1+/- mouse model and the lactate injection model,
apomorphine was not used at any stage from the start to the end of the experiment.
Instead, changes in erectile function were evaluated using intracavernous pressure
(ICP) measurements and histological examinations. Therefore, the changes in erectile
function observed in these latter two model groups can completely exclude
interference from the central effects of apomorphine, and their results directly reflect
the independent impact of metabolic alterations (Fbp1 deficiency or exogenous lactate)
on erectile function.
Second, during the screening phase of the DMED model, we ensured strict
consistency in experimental procedures. After receiving apomorphine (100 μg/kg,
subcutaneous injection). The positive erectile rate in the normal control group was
nearly 100%, which strongly confirms that the central neural pathway dependent on
apomorphine was functionally intact under our experimental conditions. If DMED or
its associated metabolic interventions (e.g., lactate accumulation) had impaired this
neural pathway, delayed or absent erectile responses should have been observed first
in the control group or during the early screening phase—but this was not the case.
This indicates that DMED-related erectile dysfunction does not originate from
primary damage to the neural control pathway.
Finally, regarding concerns about drug residue effects, apomorphine has an extremely
short elimination half-life in mice. After a single screening injection, the drug was
completely cleared long before the start of the 4-week intervention treatment with
Fbp1 C282S-LNP and other agents. Therefore, all subsequent therapeutic effects were
significantly associated with the restoration of local FBP1 activity and the reduction
of lactate levels in the corpus cavernosum. This series of results clearly indicates that
the mechanism of action stems from the correction of the local metabolic environment,
rather than sustained effects on the neural pathway revealed by the early apomorphine
test.
We again thank you for your profound insight, which has made our argument more
rigorous.
Minor concerns
1 - The authors describe H-PROTAC as a CBX3-sepcific degrader. However,
Supp Fig 5 does not demonstrate specificity. The authors did not test whether
degradation of other proteins, aside from CBX3, were altered by H-PROTAC
treatment.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the important question you raised regarding the
specificity verification of H-PROTAC. You correctly pointed out that our description
of H-PROTAC as a "CBX3-specific degrader" in the original manuscript was
insufficiently rigorous, and Supplementary Figure 9 indeed failed to fully demonstrate
its selectivity for other proteins.
As stated in our Methods section, we screened protein databases and identified that
the QTAR M3L peptide of H3K9me3 can specifically bind to CBX3—based on this
finding, we developed a degrader primarily targeting CBX3. However, we fully agree
that since CBX1, CBX3, and CBX5 all belong to the HP1 family and are all
H3K9me3 readers, this degrader may indeed exhibit a certain degree of
cross-reactivity.
In accordance with your suggestion, we have supplemented experiments to verify the
degradation effect of H-PROTAC on different CBX protein family members. The
results showed that at a concentration of 1 μM, H-PROTAC significantly degraded
CBX3, while its degradation effect on CBX1 and CBX5 was notably weaker. This
concentration gradient experiment not only provided a basis for us to select the
optimal working concentration but also confirmed that H-PROTAC exhibits relative
selectivity for CBX3 at specific concentrations.
We have revised the relevant description in the original manuscript, and supplemented
the corresponding experimental data. These revisions have made our descriptions
more accurate and our experimental design more comprehensive. We once again
thank you for your rigorous review comments, which are of great value for improving
the scientific rigor and accuracy of our research.
2 - Experiments assessing the palmitoylation status of FBP1 should include both
positive and negative controls (proteins known to be palmitoylated and known to
not be palmitoylated) to demonstrate that the assay was successful. In addition,
there should be quantitation for these experiments, and not just a representative
immunoblot.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the critical comment emphasizing the necessity of
including positive/negative controls and performing quantitative analysis in
experiments investigating FBP1 palmitoylation. We fully concur that these
recommendations are essential for ensuring the reliability of experimental results, and
systematic refinements have been implemented in the previous round of revisions.
Specifically, in the acyl-biotin exchange (ABE) assay—a gold-standard method for
detecting protein palmitoylation—we have established a comprehensive control
system: acylglycerol kinase (AGK), a well-characterized stably palmitoylated protein,
was employed as the positive control, while β-actin (for which no evidence of
palmitoylation has been reported to date) served as the negative control. This control
strategy robustly validates the efficacy of our experimental protocol.
Concurrently, rigorous quantitative analysis of palmitoylation levels was performed
across all cell line-based experiments. The full set of quantitative results has been
compiled in Supplementary Figure S11, thereby providing reliable data support for
our experimental findings. It should be noted that in primary cell experiments,
quantitative analysis is subject to certain limitations due to practical constraints,
including the difficulty in isolating primary cells and the restricted number of viable
cell passages.
Through these supplementary experiments and methodological refinements, we
believe the current experimental data substantially enhance the reliability and
persuasiveness of our FBP1 palmitoylation detection results. We would like to express our
gratitude again to the reviewer for this valuable guidance, which plays a pivotal role
in improving the methodological rigor of the present study.
3 - Typically, palmitoylation of proteins is thought to promote an interaction with
lipid membranes. Are there other examples of palmitoylation causing
structural/functional changes in cytosolic enzymes? If so, this should be
discussed.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the profound question you raised. You correctly
pointed out that palmitoylation modification is generally considered to promote the
interaction between proteins and lipid membranes. The recent studies have indeed
revealed that palmitoylation can also directly induce conformational changes in
cytoplasmic enzymes, thereby regulating their activity—and this is highly
consistent with the phenomenon we observed in FBP1 [PMID: 16945566; PMID:
16128592; PMID: 25576832].
In accordance with your suggestion, we have supplemented the relevant literature and
discussions in the Discussion section of the paper. These precedents strongly support
our finding that Zdhhc13-mediated palmitoylation at the C282 site can induce
conformational changes in FBP1, thereby affecting the accessibility of its active
center and ultimately inhibiting the gluconeogenic function of this enzyme. We
sincerely thank you for this directional suggestion, as it has placed our research in a
broader theoretical context and significantly enhanced the depth of our discussion.
4 - In general, the figure legends and in-text figure descriptions require much
more detailed information. Figure legends in particular should have details of
the experimental conditions, spelled out acronyms for the text in the figure
panels, description of the assays used for generation of each panel within the
figure, description of the statistical tests used, etc. Also many of the experiments
have an n=3. A larger sample size would increase the rigor of the study.
Response:We sincerely appreciate the valuable suggestions regarding the
improvement of figure information and the increase in sample size. We fully agree
that detailed figure legends and an adequate sample size are crucial for ensuring the
reproducibility and rigor of the study, and comprehensive revisions have been made in
accordance with the reviewer’s comments.
To address the issue of insufficiently detailed figure information, we have
systematically refined all figure legends: each legend now explicitly supplements key
experimental methods corresponding to individual subfigures, experimental
conditions, statistical methods, sample size, and the full names of all abbreviations
used in the figures. This ensures that readers can accurately understand the details of
each experimental design and analytical approach.
Regarding the sample size concern, we sincerely accept your comment. In all new
experiments conducted during this round of revisions, the sample size has been
increased to n=5. Meanwhile, it should be noted that due to constraints in
experimental timeline and resources, we were unable to supplement the sample size
for experiments already completed in the manuscript. We acknowledge that this may
affect the statistical power of some study results, for which we sincerely apologize,
and this limitation has been described in the " Limitations" section of the paper.
These improvements have significantly enhanced the transparency, reproducibility,
and credibility of our study results. We would like to thank the reviewer again for the
insightful suggestions, which have played an important role in improving the quality
of our research work.
5 - Line 75-80: The previous observation that sildenafil reduced lactate
accumulation in exercising rats does not necessarily imply a connection between
lactate metabolism and erectile function. It only suggests that PDE5 inhibition
reduces lactate accumulation caused be strenuous exercise.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the important insight. You are absolutely correct
that the previously cited observation regarding sildenafil reducing lactate
accumulation in exercised rats cannot directly establish a mechanistic link between
lactate metabolism and erectile function—it merely demonstrates that PDE5
inhibition can alleviate lactate accumulation induced by strenuous exercise. In
accordance with your suggestion, we have deleted the potentially misleading
statements in the original manuscript. We sincerely thank you for this highly
insightful correction, as this revision has significantly enhanced the logical rigor of
our discussion.
